By afternoon, the hall had stopped feeling like rehearsal space. People had paid to be there. Teren said places. I went to the wall opening, set my crutches where I could reach them, and did the one useful thing I had learned yesterday.

I listened.

Serra's line came. Not the line I expected. Close enough that I knew where we were. Different enough that I nearly answered the old one. I waited. One beat. Not for laughter. For her. She said, "And if I decide you're more trouble than you're worth?" My cue.

"You already stole me. Complaining now seems dishonest."

A laugh came from somewhere near the middle. Small. I let it go. Serra shifted. Fabric brushed wood.

"I was on a wall."

That got more. I had not planned pie. Good. I heard Marek move somewhere beyond the opening. Too early. He was not supposed to enter yet. Serra heard him too.

That was not her line. Marek answered immediately.

"My dear."

He was in. Fine. Apparently the King was here now. The scene was supposed to give Serra another exchange with Sword before he entered. That exchange contained the information that she intended to use me against him. We needed that. I knew we needed that.

I also had no idea how to put it back without announcing that we had missed it. Serra did. She said to Marek, "I was just telling your sword what I intend to do with him." Marek said, "My sword?" There. Fixed. No pause. No panic. The missing information was back. I almost admired it enough to miss my next line. Almost.

The audience laughed. Marek crossed closer. I could hear his shoes.

"You cannot keep it."

"I am."

"You see what I endure?" Marek asked me.

"Yes."

I waited half a breath.

"You."

A bigger laugh. Marek made a wounded sound. The room opened. I felt it. Did not chase it. Serra continued. We reached the return threat differently. Not "Perhaps I should return you." Instead she said, "He seems to want you." Marek said, "Naturally." I said, "That is not what I heard." The laugh was smaller. Fine. Serra said, "Would you prefer I melt you?" There it was. Not Marek. Her. Different again. I said, "Into what?" She paused. I knew what she could say. Spoon.

The audience from last night might remember. Some of them were probably here. I waited for her answer. Serra said, "A chamber pot." The room broke. I did too. Not aloud. Almost. Marek said, "That is my sword." Serra said, "Then you may empty him." More laughter. I had no line. None. Three possible answers arrived. All of them wanted the laugh. I discarded them.

"Put me back on the wall."

That was enough. Not huge. Enough. We moved. The scene survived. Later, I missed a cue anyway. Not because I was watching Serra. Because someone backstage dropped something metal and my attention went there. Serra covered without looking toward me.

"Have you nothing to say?"

"Yes."

I spoke the line. Late. The audience never knew. Maybe. Then the scene was over. Serra came through the wing breathing hard. I said, "Chamber pot?" She said, "Spoon was yesterday." Then Nessa grabbed her.

"Stop."

"What?"

"Back."

Serra turned. A seam had opened beneath one arm. Not much. Enough. Nessa shoved a needle through fabric while Serra still wore the dress.

"Don't stab me."

"Then stop breathing."

"That seems excessive."

"Arm."

Serra lifted it. Marek came offstage behind us.

"Chamber pot?"

"Fuck off," Serra said.

"That was excellent."

Nessa said, "Hold this." Marek held fabric. He stopped being King immediately. I moved because someone said, "Move." A local worker passed carrying a lamp. The show continued. I could hear Orin onstage. Different scene. Different problem. He spoke a line. Silence. Then another. A woman answered. Wrong line. I knew because I had heard the scene enough. Orin answered the wrong line as though it were right. She froze. He walked toward her. Not threatening. Giving her something.

Her face changed. I could see them through a gap now. She understood.

Back. The scene found its road again. No one applauded the repair. They did not know it had happened. That was probably the point. I had time before Shopkeeper. Not much. I drank water. A boy from local crew ran past.

"I enjoy disappointment."

A laugh. Still no constable. We needed him because he broke the argument and delivered the notice that moved Iven into the next scene. I did not know the notice. Iven did. He walked toward the entrance.

I had nothing useful.

"Debt."

"That is not a crime."

The constable burst in. Late. Hat sideways.

"Stop!"

Iven turned.

"For debt?"

The constable had no idea what he meant.

"No."

The audience laughed. The constable recovered.

"For disturbing the peace."

I said, "Take him." Iven said, "Him?" The constable pointed at me.

That was wrong. Very wrong. I looked at him. He looked at me. Iven looked delighted.

"Excellent," he said.

The audience laughed. The constable realized.

"No. Him."

He pointed at Iven. Too late. I said, "Professional error." The audience laughed harder than the first time. Iven put out his hands. The constable delivered the notice. We were back. The scene ended. I got offstage. The constable actor grabbed my arm.

"Sorry."

"Why me?"

"What?"

"I don't know."

Then he ran because he had another entrance. Iven came through laughing.

"You."

"Fuck you."

"You should have been arrested."

"Professional error."

I hated him. I was also laughing. Teren passed.

"Good."

The rest of the show happened around me more than to me. Backstage, repairs happened without becoming emergencies. Nessa fixed Serra while Serra was still wearing the dress. Pell changed a hem on an actress standing on a box. Davin vanished beneath the stage with a hammer and the loose board stopped making noise. The replacement for the broken blue poison jar was brown. The audience accepted that brown was poison.

Orin came offstage furious because people had laughed at his death. Marek forgot a name and called the man "my loyal friend" until the correct name returned. None of it stopped the play. Nobody congratulated the recovery because the recovery was the job.

By the final act, everyone was tired enough to stop giving slow scenes room to remain slow. Then Marek sat on a chair and the chair folded under him. The audience screamed, then laughed.

"Water."

"Where's the red dress?"

"Don't sit there."

"Who has my shoe?"

"Move the bench."

"Gate count?"

"Later."

"Coln."

Of course. I drank water. My shirt stuck to my back. My hands shook slightly from work and heat. Serra sat on the floor while Nessa removed the damaged sleeve. Marek had a scrape on one palm from the chair. Iven was eating bread already. Orin was still offended by his death.

The first tavern was full. Marek opened the door, looked inside, and said, "No."

"You said first one."

"I was wrong."

"That was fast."

"I improve."

Iven walked into my back with the bottle.

"Why are we stopped?"

"Marek has standards."

"Since when?"

"Tonight."

Marek shut the door. A man inside shouted his name before it closed. Marek kept walking.

"You know him?" I asked.

"No."

"He knew you."

"Common problem."

The second tavern had music. Not good music. Still music. A fiddle, a drum, and a woman singing loudly enough that quality had become less important than commitment. The windows were open to the river. Light spilled across the street in yellow blocks. People stood outside with cups because there was nowhere left to sit. Marek stopped.

"Yes."

Iven said, "Too loud."

"Yes."

"That wasn't approval."

Marek went in. We followed. The room smelled like beer, hot bodies, fried onions, river damp, and smoke. Someone had moved two tables against a wall to make space near the musicians. Nobody was dancing exactly. Several people were failing to stand still. A woman near the door saw Marek.

"King!"

He bowed.

"Citizen."

"You owe me money."

He straightened.

"I have never seen you before."

"You borrowed four coppers from me three years ago."

Marek looked at her. Then at me.

"Local history."

She held out her hand. He paid her. Iven laughed so hard he had to lean against the wall. The woman bit one of the coins.

"Interest."

"No."

"Five years."

"You said three."

"Interest."

"That is not how---"

She took another coin from his hand while he argued. Then kissed his cheek.

"Good show."

She disappeared into the room. I stared. Marek wiped his cheek.

"Local history."

"I said nothing."

"Good."

Iven was still laughing. We found a table because Orin already had one. Of course. He sat with the man from River House, two women I did not know, and a narrow man with silver rings on three fingers. Four cups and a deck of cards occupied the center. Orin pointed at us.

"Late."

"We left before you," Marek said.

"Yes."

"How?"

Orin shrugged. The man from River House moved his chair enough to make room for Iven. Nobody moved for me. I looked around. A stool stood near the wall. I got it. Marek shouted toward the bar, "Four!" I said, "Three." He looked at me.

"You are here."

"I can buy mine."

He considered.

"Five!"

"That is worse."

A server appeared carrying cups. Not because Marek had shouted. She was already coming. She put one in front of Orin, one in front of the silver-ringed man, and two at another table. Marek watched them go.

"Betrayal."

The server returned.

"What?"

"Four beers."

"Pay."

Marek pointed at me.

"No."

She looked at me. I said, "One."

"Coward," Marek said.

"I am buying one."

"That is how it starts."

The server named a price. I reached into my pocket. For the first time, I spent money I had earned by being a sword and a shopkeeper. The coin looked exactly like every other coin. Good. I gave it to her. She gave me change. Also ordinary. Better. Marek paid for his and Iven's. Orin already had one.

The server looked at the fifth empty place Marek had apparently ordered for. Marek said, "Future." She left. I drank. Beer. Not terrible. Not good. Cold enough. I had expected something. "No."

"Excellent."

Marek turned.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Roof?"

"Nothing."

"No."

Orin turned to me.

"Do you see what I endure?"

I said, "Again." The woman laughed. Orin pointed at me.

"Traitor."

I was enjoying myself. That surprised me enough that I noticed. Then I stopped noticing. Someone dragged the table back two feet because dancing had become real. Nobody asked. The cards moved with it. A cup spilled. The silver-ringed man swore. A woman stepped onto a bench to sing. Not one of the musicians. Just a woman. People joined. I knew none of the words. Marek reappeared beside me.

"Stand."

"No."

"Dance."

"No."

"You have one leg."

"I am aware."

"Excellent excuse."

"For not dancing."

"For dancing badly."

He grabbed my wrist. I did not move. He pulled. Still no.

"Marek."

"Gregory."

"No."

He let go immediately.

"Fine."

Then danced badly beside me. Not mockingly. Just badly. He had both legs and apparently no plan for either. I laughed. A woman joined him. Then another man. Then Iven. Iven was worse. That helped. I stayed on the stool. My shoulders hurt less now that the crutches leaned against the wall. My hands wrapped around the cup. Someone bumped my right foot. Apologized. Someone else stepped on Marek. Did not apologize. The song sped up. Marek nearly fell. He recovered by grabbing Iven. Iven nearly fell. They both shouted.

The room cheered for reasons unrelated to them. I drank. A second beer appeared. I had not ordered it. I looked around. The server pointed toward the bar. The constable actor from the show raised his cup. I raised mine. Free beer. Marek had been right. Terrible. I drank that one too. Slower. The constable actor came over later.

"Sorry again."

"For arresting me?"

"Trying."

"You got it right tonight."

"Boring."

"Yes."

He leaned on the table.

"My brother saw afternoon. Told everyone I arrested the one-legged shopkeeper."

"You did."

"I know."

"He made it sound intentional?"

"Yes."

"Better story."

He nodded. Then someone called him. He left. No name. I realized I still did not know his name. I could ask later. Or not. The theatre had many people I knew by mistakes. That seemed normal now. The front door opened. Teren came in. The room noticed less than I expected. Our table noticed. Orin lifted his cup.

"Money?"

Teren looked at him.

"You already got paid."

"More?"

"No."

Orin lowered the cup. Teren went to the bar. He did not sit with us. He spoke to the tavern keeper. Then a man I did not know joined him. They talked. Not happily. Not angrily. Business. Marek saw.

"Tomorrow."

"What?"

He pointed.

"Booking."

"How do you know?"

"I don't."

"Then why---"

"Could be debt."

"Whose?"

"Yes."

I stopped asking. Teren eventually got a drink. One. He stood at the end of the bar with it. Nobody dragged him into the party. Maybe because he would refuse. Maybe because they knew better. After a while, Rinna came in. Alone.

She looked around, found Orin, said something in his ear, took his drink, finished it, and left. Orin stared after her.

"What was that?"

The green-scarf woman asked.

"Work."

"What work?"

"Not mine."

He dealt. I liked that answer. Davin arrived perhaps an hour later. Grease on both sleeves now. He came through the door, found us, and sat without removing his coat. Marek put a beer in front of him. Davin drank half.

"Box?" I asked.

He looked at me. I regretted it.

"Dry."

"Good."

He drank the rest. Marek said, "Stay."

"No."

"You just arrived."

"Yes."

"Where are you going?"

"Sleep."

"Coward."

Davin stood.

"Wheel at seven."

"What wheel?"

Davin left. Marek looked at me.

"Local history."

"You don't know either."

"No."

Good. No Serra. I noticed because I was not looking for her. That was probably a lie. I saw yellow at the door once and looked. Different woman. Fine. Lyssa came into my head unexpectedly when a couple near the wall began arguing. Not because they resembled us. They did not.

The woman was short and furious. The man kept eating while she spoke. I thought Lyssa would have hated Marek. Then I thought no, she might like him for twenty minutes. Then hate him. Then maybe like him again. I smiled into my cup. Marek saw.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Woman?"

"Yes."

He looked around.

"Which?"

"Not here."

He understood.

"Oh."

That was all. No teasing. Interesting. Then he stole one of my remaining coins. I slapped his hand.

"Fuck you."

"There he is."

I took the coin back. The music changed again. Slower. People paired off. Some left. Some moved closer. Iven was talking to a man by the window with both hands, serious now. Orin's River House friend had disappeared. The green-scarf woman leaned against Orin's shoulder while still beating him at cards. The silver-ringed man had acquired another deck somehow. Teren was gone. I had not seen him leave. Marek vanished again. This time with the woman who had slapped his shoulder earlier. Maybe.

I saw them go toward the back. Could have been anything. Not mine. I bought food. Fried potatoes. Too salty. Perfect. I paid with show money. That felt better than beer. I ate half. Gave the rest to Iven when he returned.

"Why?"

"I can't finish."

He took them. No ceremony.

"Tomorrow," he said.

"What?"

"Leave after noon."

"For Carrow?"

"No."

I waited. He ate.

"Where?"

"North."

"How far?"

"Day."

"Show?"

"Maybe."

"Maybe?"

"Teren's talking."

"Of course."

Iven ate another potato.

"Could be two nights. Could be nothing."

"When will we know?"

"Before we leave."

"That is not enough time."

"For what?"

I had no answer. Packing. Knowing. Preparing. Apparently none required much.

"What about tomorrow morning?"

"Sleep."

"That I can do."

"Then you're ready."

He left with the potatoes. There. Tomorrow. Not rehearsal. Maybe travel. Maybe another town. Maybe another show. I did not know. The uncertainty bothered me less than it should have. Or maybe the beer helped. I stood carefully. Two beers. Not drunk. Different. My head felt warm. My body was still tired beneath it. My hands had stopped hurting because I was not using them. That would change as soon as I picked up the crutches. I did. Yes. Still tired. Marek returned. His hair was worse.

"River House."

"You're leaving?"

"Eventually."

"You look terrible."

"Successful."

"Different word."

"Same profession."

He had lost money. I knew because he checked his pocket, frowned, checked another, then smiled as though this had been expected.

"How much did you spend?"

"No."

"How much?"

"No."

"Do you know?"

He thought.

"No."

I laughed. He pointed at me.

"New man laughs."

"Old man loses money."

"I am twenty-four."

"Ancient."

"Cruel."

We found Iven near the door. Orin refused to leave.

"Winning," he said.

The green-scarf woman said, "Losing."

"Strategically."

We left him. Outside, the river air hit cold. Good. The street had emptied some. Not much. People still moved between taverns. A cart rattled over stones. Somewhere upriver, somebody sang badly without accompaniment. Iven walked ahead. Marek walked beside me for half a block, then stopped to talk to a man sitting on a windowsill. I kept going. He caught up.

"Who was that?" I asked.

"No idea."

"You stopped."

"He knew me."

"Did you know him?"

"Now."

That might have been true. River House appeared after one wrong turn. Marek blamed Iven. Iven had not been with us for the wrong turn. He had gone the correct way. We found him at the front door.

"Idiots."

"Traitor," Marek said.

Inside, the desk woman looked at us.

"No singing."

"We are not singing," Marek said.

"No fighting."

"We are friends."

She looked at me. I said, "Probably."

"No breaking furniture."

Marek looked offended.

"That was the hall."

Her eyes narrowed. We went upstairs. Room one was dark. Pell was asleep. Or unconscious. Hard to tell. I moved quietly. Not carefully. Different. My purse went beneath my folded trousers. Then I took it back out. Counted what remained. Two show payments. Minus beer. Minus cards. Minus food. Still most of it. Good. I put it away. I washed my face. Cleaned up enough. Checked my leg. Fine. Too tired for anything more complicated. Pell spoke from the dark.

"Red."

I froze.

"What?"

"Dress."

"Are you awake?"

"No."

"Is it done?"

"No."

Then he snored. Fine. I lay down. The room moved slightly when I closed my eyes. Not spinning. Considering it. I opened them. Waited. Closed them again. Better. Downstairs, someone laughed. A door shut. Footsteps crossed the hall. Then more footsteps. The troupe had not all come home. Maybe some would not. Tomorrow after noon we might leave north. Maybe for another show. Maybe not. I had no idea what the town was called. That seemed like information I should possess. I could ask in the morning.

I thought about the money beneath my trousers. Not all of it. Most. Enough. I had spent some because I wanted to. Beer. Cards. Potatoes. Stupid things. Mine. I smiled in the dark. Then somebody in the next room began snoring hard enough to shake the wall. I threw a pillow at it. The wall did not care. Pell did not wake. I laughed once. Quietly. Then slept.
CHAPTER 154
THE VISITOR

Someone was hammering inside my skull. I opened my eyes. The hammer stopped. A second later it started again. Not my skull. Outside. Somewhere below the window, metal struck metal three times, paused, then struck twice more. Pell was already awake. That offended me.

He sat on the edge of his bed with the red dress across his knees and a needle between his teeth.

"What time is it?"

He took the needle out.

"Morning."

"Useful."

"You asked."

My mouth tasted like old beer and sleep. My shoulders had stiffened overnight. Both hands felt thick when I flexed them. Nothing terrible. Just everything reminding me it had been used yesterday. Pell bent over the dress.

"You came in loud."

"I did not."

"You argued with the wall."

"The wall was snoring."

"That was room two."

"Then room two was snoring through the wall."

Pell considered.

"Fair."

I sat up. The room moved exactly once. Then stopped. Good. Two beers. Apparently two beers had opinions. I drank from the water cup beside the bed. Warm. Excellent.

"Did you finish it?"

Pell looked down at the red dress.

"No."

"You were working on it when I went out."

"Nessa was."

"You were asleep when I came back."

"Yes."

"And now you're working on it."

"Yes."

"When do you stop?"

"When it stops being wrong."

"That sounds dangerous."

He put the needle back between his teeth. I got dressed. My residual limb was warm but normal. The wrapping had shifted slightly overnight. I redid it before standing. No problem. My hands objected to the crutches. They lost. Downstairs, River House had become a collection of consequences. Marek was facedown on a table. Not asleep. I knew because when I entered he lifted one finger.

"Water."

A pitcher sat six inches from his hand. I pushed it closer. He did not move.

"Closer."

"It is touching you."

"Cruel."

I poured a cup and put it beside his head. He turned enough to drink without sitting up.

"Thank you."

"You spent all your money?"

"No."

"How much is left?"

He closed his eyes.

"Do not attack me."

"I asked a question."

"Violence."

Iven sat by the window eating eggs. He looked fine. I disliked him for that.

"You drank more than I did."

"Yes."

"Why are you fine?"

"I am older."

"That should make it worse."

"Experience."

"No."

"Water."

"I drank water."

"More."

I got breakfast. Eggs, bread, something fried, more water. Orin was absent. Serra was absent. Teren was absent. Rinna came through the front door while I ate, carrying a small paper packet and three lengths of cord. She looked as though she had been awake for hours.

"Morning," I said.

She looked at me.

"Is it?"

Then she went upstairs. Marek lifted his head.

"Rinna."

She did not turn.

"Rinna."

Nothing.

"Rinna, I require medical aid."

From upstairs:

"Die quietly."

Marek put his face back on the table. Iven ate. The hammering outside stopped. Then Davin came in. So that explained nothing. He had grease on one cheek and a wooden wedge in his hand.

"Wheel?" I asked.

"Yes."

"Fixed?"

"No."

He took bread.

"Broken?"

"No."

I waited. He ate.

"Then what is wrong with it?"

"Wrong wheel."

I stared.

"You got up at seven for the wrong wheel?"

"No."

He left. Marek said into the table, "Davin conversations are very satisfying." I agreed. Teren arrived twenty minutes later with Serra. Not together exactly. They entered through the same door. Serra had her hair tied back and looked tired but clean. Teren looked like he had slept in a chair while negotiating with it. Neither explained where they had been. Good. Teren put a folded paper on the breakfast table.

"North after noon."

Iven kept eating. Marek raised his head.

"Show?"

"Tomorrow night."

"Money?"

"If we perform."

"That sounds conditional."

"It is."

"Why?"

"Because they have not seen the hall yet."

"Who?"

"We."

Marek frowned. Teren drank from the pitcher.

"The booking is offered. Hall is supposedly usable. We arrive tonight, look at it, perform tomorrow if it is not a barn."

"Barns pay," Iven said.

"Not this rate."

Marek sat upright. That appeared to hurt him.

"How much?"

Teren told him. Not me. Quiet enough that I missed it. Marek's face improved.

"Good hall."

"We haven't seen it."

"Excellent hall."

Teren ignored him.

"One day north. Two nights likely. Maybe three if tomorrow sells. We leave at one."

There. A job. Maybe. No rehearsal. No speech. I ate another piece of bread. Teren pointed at me.

"Gregory."

"Yes?"

"You coming?"

I looked at him. That was somehow still a question.

"Yes."

"Good."

He went upstairs. Serra took the chair opposite me. I said, "Morning."

"Is it?"

"Rinna said that."

"Rinna is wise."

She stole half my bread. Apparently this was universal. I did not ask where she had been. She did not tell me. Marek looked between us. Then thought better of whatever he was about to say. Progress for everyone. Packing began at ten. Not because anyone announced it. Things simply started leaving River House. Costume trunks went first.

Rinna and Pell carried one between them. I moved toward the other end. Rinna said, "No." I stopped. She pointed with her chin.

"Door."

I opened the door. Useful. The next trunk came. I held the door. Then another. I was excellent at doors. Outside, two wagons waited. One had a wheel removed. Davin sat beside it with three wheels. Three. I stared. He noticed.

"Leave the wheels."

"I said nothing."

"Good." He selected one wheel, rolled it upright, looked at the hub, and rejected it.

"What was wrong with the first wheel?"

"Nothing."

"Then why---"

"Other wagon."

I looked at the second wagon. It had four wheels. I decided not every wheel needed to become mine. Davin glanced up.

"Good."

I hated that he knew. The long iron-cornered box emerged from the hall later, not River House. Two local workers and Davin brought it. Still closed. Still upright. Still apparently more important than its contents. They loaded it against the inner wagon rail and tied it in place. I watched the knot. Recognized enough to know I should not touch it. Also progress. Coln stood outside the hall with Teren. They spoke briefly. No shouting. No visible murder. Teren handed him something. Coln counted it.

Marek saw Coln and immediately crossed to the far side of the wagon. I said, "Subtle."

"Learn from masters."

"Does he still hate you?"

"He has excellent taste."

"That does not answer me."

"It answered something."

Coln looked over. Marek waved. Coln did not. Serra walked past both of them carrying a basket. Neither stopped her. The yellow-scarf woman was not there. I noticed. Then stopped noticing. Mostly. By eleven, the red dress finally left River House. Not finished.

I knew because Nessa walked behind Pell while he carried it and said, "Don't fold that."

"I am not."

"You are thinking about it."

"I am carrying it."

"Like you intend to fold it."

"How does that look different?"

"It does."

They disappeared toward the hall. Marek watched.

"I am glad I am not a dress."

"You would be a terrible dress."

"Excellent legs."

"One of us has to be realistic."

He looked at mine. Then at me. I raised a crutch. He moved away. I packed my own bag. That part was easier now. Not easy. Less stupid. Shirt. Wrapping. Food. The few things I had brought. My money went into the inner pocket rather than the top of the bag. I tied my crutches to the wagon myself. Slipped hitch. Test. Release. Retie. Done. No one watched. Better. Then I put my bag in the wrong wagon. Rinna took it out.

"Other."

"Why?"

"This is costumes."

"There are boots in it."

"Costume boots."

"There is bread."

"Not ours."

I took my bag.

"Other wagon?"

"Yes."

I moved it. Veteran. At noon, Orin appeared. No coat. One shoe muddy. He carried a small wrapped parcel. Nobody asked where he had been. Marek did.

"Where were you?"

Orin looked at him.

"No."

"What happened to your coat?"

"No."

"Why is your shoe---"

"No."

"What is in the parcel?"

Orin put the parcel into his bag.

"No."

Marek turned to me.

"Local history."

Orin said, "I will kill you."

"See? History."

The green-scarf woman did not appear. Neither did his River House friend. Again, not mine. We were almost ready when the visitor arrived. I noticed him because he did not fit anything. Not rich exactly. Not poor. Not local crew. Not hall. Not inn. Not audience, as far as I remembered.

He was perhaps fifty. Maybe older. Thin gray coat despite the warmth. Dark gloves. A narrow face with one eyebrow that rose slightly higher than the other even when he was not making an expression. He carried no bag. That was the first odd thing. Travelers carried things. Workers carried things. People leaving inns carried things. He carried a walking stick he did not seem to need. He stopped across the street. Looked at the wagons. Looked at the hall. Looked at me. Not stared. Looked. Then away.

I kept tying my bag. A minute later he crossed.

"Excuse me."

I looked up. He was closer now. His coat had good stitching and bad buttons. One button was wood. The others horn.

"Yes?"

"You're the sword."

I waited.

"Sometimes."

His mouth moved slightly. Not a smile.

"You were the shopkeeper too."

"Yes."

"Twice."

"Yes."

"You changed him."

I did not know what he meant.

"Between shows."

"Oh."

He waited. I waited. The street moved around us. A cart passed. Somebody shouted from the hall. Marek laughed at something behind the wagon. The man said, "Which was closer?"

"To what?"

"The role."

I looked at him.

"I don't know."

"Good."

That irritated me.

"What is good?"

"That answer."

"Why?"

He glanced toward the hall.

"Most people would choose."

"I can choose if you want."

"No."

He looked at my crutches. Not my leg. The crutches. Then at the wagon knot. Then at my hands.

"Do you always play seated roles?"

"No."

"What else?"

"Sword."

"That is not seated."

"It is mounted."

That almost got the smile.

"Fair."

I said, "Who are you?"

"Lucan Drell."

The name meant nothing. He seemed unsurprised.

"Greg."

"I know."

That was less comfortable.

"From the show?"

"From several conversations."

"With who?"

"People."

"Useful."

This time he smiled. Small.

"There you are."

"What?"

"Nothing."

I disliked him. Not enough to leave. He asked, "How long have you been with them?"

"I am not sure I am with them."

He looked at the wagons. Then at my bag. Then at the crutches tied to the rail.

"Of course."

"That sounded like disagreement."

"It was observation."

"Those are usually worse."

He laughed once. Quietly. Marek appeared beside me. Not protectively. Curiously.

"Friend?"

"No."

Lucan looked at him.

"King."

Marek bowed.

"Sometimes."

Lucan said, "You were better at night." Marek's expression changed. Not much.

"You saw both."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"I had tickets."

"That is suspicious."

"I bought them."

"Worse."

Lucan looked back at me.

"You listen more when you're tired."

I felt something tighten. Not fear. Annoyance. Maybe because it was too close to something I had been doing.

"I also miss more lines."

"Yes."

"That seems relevant."

"It is."

Marek said, "Are you hiring him?" I turned.

"What?"

Lucan's eyebrow rose.

"No."

"Then stop interviewing him."

"I wasn't."

"You're bad at it."

Lucan considered Marek.

"Possibly."

Marek leaned toward me.

"Strange man."

"He is standing here."

"I know."

Lucan did not seem offended. That made him stranger. Teren came out of the hall. Saw Lucan. Stopped. Not dramatically. Just stopped. Then continued toward us.

"Drell."

"Teren."

They knew each other. Of course. Marek looked delighted.

"Local history."

Teren ignored him.

"What do you want?"

"Nothing."

"Then you're expensive."

Lucan smiled again.

"I watched your shows."

"I heard."

"From whom?"

"Coln."

Lucan looked toward the hall.

"Still alive."

"Unfortunately."

"Still charging for air?"

"By the breath."

That was the most relaxed I had seen Teren with Coln's name involved. Not friendly. Familiar. Lucan tapped his walking stick once against the stones.

"You have the old box."

Everything near me seemed to get quieter. It did not. The street was still loud. But I heard that. Teren said, "Yes." Marek stopped smiling. Lucan looked at the wagon. The long box was partly visible behind the rail.

"Still upright."

"Davin."

"Of course."

"What do you want, Drell?"

Lucan looked at me again.

"Nothing today."

Today. I did not like that word. Teren did not either.

"You're not taking anyone."

"I didn't ask."

"Good."

Marek said, "Taking?" Nobody answered him. Excellent. Lucan said to me, "North?" I looked at Teren. Teren's face said nothing.

"I think so."

"Good road after the ridge. Bad before."

"Thank you."

"Don't thank him," Teren said.

"Why?"

"He'll think you owe him."

Lucan nodded.

"True."

I definitely disliked him now. He stepped back.

"Safe road."

Marek said, "No." Lucan looked at him.

"You don't get to arrive strangely, ask questions, know Teren, mention the box, stare at Gregory, and then leave."

Lucan considered this.

"Yes."

"That is exactly what you are doing."

"Yes."

"Who are you?"

"I told him."

"You did not tell me."

"Lucan Drell."

Marek waited.

"So?"

"So what?"

"What does that mean?"

"Usually that someone wants my attention."

Marek looked at me.

"I hate him."

"I was ahead of you."

Lucan actually laughed. Then he left. Just walked away. No carriage. No companion. No explanation. He went uphill and disappeared into the noon crowd. Marek watched him.

"Follow?"

"No," Teren said.

"I wasn't asking you."

"No," I said.

Marek sighed.

"Cowards."

Teren looked at me.

"If he speaks to you again, tell me."

"Why?"

"Because I asked."

"That is not a reason."

"It is the one you have."

He walked toward the wagon. I followed him two steps.

"Teren."

He stopped.

"Who is he?"

"Drell."

"I know his name."

"Then you're ahead."

"Is he theatre?"

"No."

"Guild?"

Teren looked at me.

"No."

That answer came fast enough that I believed it.

"What does he want?"

"If I knew, I would have told him no more specifically."

That sounded true.

"Why did you say he isn't taking anyone?"

Teren rubbed his face.

"Tired."

"That was not an answer."

"No."

He walked away. Fine. Not mine. Except apparently slightly mine. I hated that. At one, we left. Not exactly at one. One fifteen. Which counted. Marek slept almost immediately. He took the side bench, folded his arms, and disappeared. Iven sat opposite me with his hat over his eyes. Orin rode in the other wagon. Serra had somehow acquired an apple. I did not ask from where.

Pell and Nessa remained in a quiet argument about the red dress until the wagon moved, then both stopped because sewing on the road was apparently a form of suicide. Rinna counted coins into three separate cloth packets. One went into her bag. One into a costume trunk. One she gave to Pell. He did not count it. Davin drove. The correct wheel stayed on. I assumed. The town thinned. Stone became packed road. River stayed with us for a while, then bent away. North. The road climbed.

Lucan had said bad before the ridge. He was right. That annoyed me too. The wagon jolted hard enough to wake Marek. He opened one eye.

"Drell."

"What?"

"Who?"

"I don't know."

"Teren knows."

"Yes."

"Box."

"Yes."

"Taking."

"Yes."

We sat with that. Then Marek said, "Beer."

"No."

"Last night."

"Yes."

"Good."

"Are you changing subjects?"

"Yes."

"Thank you."

He went back to sleep. I looked out at the road. Fields. Low stone walls. A woman leading two goats. A boy sitting on a gate. Clouds collecting farther north. The wagon hit another rut. My shoulder hit the side. I swore. Serra handed me the apple. I looked at it.

"For me?"

"No."

"Then why?"

"Hold."

She retied her hair. I held the apple. Then she took it back. Fine. Hours passed. Not interesting hours. Good hours. We stopped once for water. Davin checked the wheel. The mysterious one. Or a different one. I did not ask. At the stop, Teren spoke with a courier heading south. The courier handed him a folded note. Teren read it. Swore. Marek woke instantly.

"Money?"

"No."

"Show?"

"Maybe."

"That was already maybe."

"Now differently maybe."

"What happened?"

Teren folded the note.

"Hall has a roof leak."

I laughed. Everyone looked at me.

"What?"

Marek pointed.

"Roof boy."

"Fuck you."

Teren said, "If the stage is wet, we don't perform."

"Can it be moved?" I asked.

"Maybe."

"To where?"

"Gregory."

"Yes?"

"Don't become interested."

"I am not."

"You are visibly interested."

"My face?"

"Yes."

Everyone was right about my face. We continued north. The rain started before the ridge. Not much. Enough to make everyone look at the sky. Teren looked at it longest. A hall with a roof leak. A maybe show. A strange man named Lucan Drell who had watched me twice, knew Teren, knew the box, and apparently thought I listened better when tired. I decided not to think about him. That worked for almost four minutes. Then the wagon hit another rut. Marek woke again.

"Are we there?"

"No."

"Wake me when money."

He slept. I laughed. Then looked north. Another town. Maybe another show. Maybe a wet stage. Apparently that was tomorrow's problem.
CHAPTER 155
THE TROUBLESHOOTER

The rain improved. By improved, I mean it stopped hitting me in the face. It continued hitting everything else. We came over the ridge near evening with the wagon wheels cutting dark lines through the road and water running in the ditches on both sides. The northern country opened below us in wet fields, low walls, and trees bent by wind. Somewhere beyond them sat the town. Marek woke. He looked at the sky.

"No."

Then he went back to sleep. Serra had eaten the apple. I had seen none of it happen. The core was in her hand.

"You could have given me some."

"You were thinking."

"That does not prevent eating."

"It should."

She threw the core into the ditch. The wagon dropped into a rut. My shoulder hit the side again. Drell had been right about the road. I disliked him more for every mile. I had decided not to think about Lucan Drell.

This remained a poor decision because deciding not to think about someone required checking periodically whether I was thinking about him. I made it almost ten minutes once. Then Marek woke again.

"Strange man."

"Go to sleep."

"I was."

"You failed."

He rubbed his face. "Did Teren tell you anything?"

"No."

"Good. Me neither."

"That is not good."

"It means I remain important."

"How?"

"He withholds information from important people."

"He withholds information from everyone."

Marek considered.

"I am extremely important."

I looked out at the rain. The town appeared through it gradually. First a church tower. Then smoke. Then roofs. Mostly dark tile, some thatch at the edges, chimneys sending smoke sideways in the wind. One roof near the center had a blue tarp stretched over part of it. I stared. Serra followed my eyes.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"You leaned."

"I am sitting."

"You leaned while sitting."

"My face and my body are both apparently treacherous."

"Yes."

The road narrowed between houses. People had laid boards across the worst mud near doorways. Water came off roofs in sheets where gutters failed. A woman in an apron stood under an awning arguing with a man who had three chickens tucked inside his coat. The chickens looked dry. He did not. Our wagon stopped. Then started. Then stopped again. Davin shouted something to the other wagon. Someone shouted back. I could not hear either of them. Teren got down. That meant we were either here or in trouble.

Usually both. The hall stood at the end of a market street. It was not the building with the blue tarp. I felt betrayed. It was lower and wider, built of brick on a stone foundation, with a long roof sloping toward the street and three tall front windows. A covered entry projected from one side. The sign above the main doors had once been painted green. Water dripped from every edge. Two men were on the roof.

One of them was kneeling beside a ladder with a roll of something dark. The other held a bucket. Inside the front doors, another bucket caught water. Marek climbed down from the wagon. He looked at the bucket.

"Money?"

Teren turned.

"Not yet."

Marek looked genuinely wounded. A woman came through the doors carrying a second bucket. She was short, broad through the shoulders, with her sleeves rolled above both elbows despite the cold.

"You're late."

Teren looked at the rain. She looked at the rain.

"Fine," she said. "You're here."

"Teren."

"Bessa."

They shook hands. Bessa looked at the wagons.

"Keep the trunks under cover."

Nessa was already saying the same thing.

"Costumes first. Pell, no. That side. Rinna, where is the oilcloth?"

"In the wagon."

"Which?"

Rinna stared at her. Nessa closed her eyes.

"Fine."

The company exploded. I got down carefully. The mud was deep enough that my left crutch sank farther than expected. I nearly followed it. I did not. I pulled it free, found stone near the edge of the road, and moved toward the hall. Davin pointed at me.

"Door."

I knew doors. I held it. Costume trunk. Prop crate. Another trunk. Basket. Three rolled cloths. The long box came last. Davin and two local men carried it between them. Still closed. Still upright once they put it inside. Bessa looked at it.

"What is that?"

"Dry," Davin said.

She waited. He did not add anything.

"Does it need a room?"

"Yes."

"Everything needs a room."

"Dry room."

She looked at Teren. Teren said, "Later." Good. The old box had returned to being someone else's problem. I went inside. The hall smelled of wet brick, lamp oil, old wood, and the particular damp smell of a room that had been closed while rain happened above it. The main room was bigger than I expected.

Benches filled most of the floor. A low stage ran across the far end, perhaps three feet high, with shallow wings and a rear curtain hung from a timber frame. There was no proper fly space. No high scenery. No upper gallery. There were also seven buckets. I counted. Then found an eighth.

"Don't," Teren said behind me.

"I am counting buckets."

"That is the beginning."

"The beginning of what?"

He walked past. Bessa stood near the stage with another man. This one had gray hair tied at the back and wet knees on his trousers. He pointed upward.

"The beam is fine."

Bessa said, "The beam is wet."

"The beam has been wet before."

"That is not the defense you think it is."

Teren joined them.

"Stage?"

Bessa pointed. The left rear quarter of the stage was covered by a canvas sheet. Water had darkened it in several places. One bucket sat on top. Another sat behind the curtain.

"That's the worst," she said.

Teren climbed onto the stage. I stayed below. Mostly. He walked the dry section. Pressed his heel against two boards. Looked up.

"How long?"

The gray-haired man said, "Roof patch tonight if the wind drops."

"If it doesn't?"

"Morning."

"If it doesn't in the morning?"

The man shrugged. Bessa said, "It will." Teren looked at her. She corrected herself.

"It usually does."

Marek appeared beside me.

"Money?"

"You asked already."

"I am checking."

Teren heard him.

"If we can use the room."

"Can we?"

Teren pointed at the wet stage. Marek considered.

"Other half."

Bessa laughed. Teren did not.

"How many sold?"

"Forty-two already."

That changed Teren's face slightly. Not happiness. Arithmetic.

"Capacity?"

"Normally one twenty."

"With that side closed?"

Bessa looked at the benches.

"Ninety."

The gray-haired man said, "Hundred."

"Ninety," Bessa repeated.

"Hundred if they're friendly."

"They paid for a show, not marriage."

Marek said, "Ninety is money." Teren looked at him. Marek raised both hands.

"Professional contribution."

Teren turned back to Bessa.

"If the stage stays like this, we lose that entrance."

"Yes."

"And the rear cross."

"Yes."

"Curtain?"

"Can stay."

The gray-haired man said, "Probably." Teren looked up. The man sighed.

"Can stay."

"Dressing?"

"Two rooms behind. One leaks at the window, not the roof."

"Props?"

"Store room."

"Dry?"

Bessa looked toward Davin.

"Dry enough."

Davin, from across the room, said, "No." Everyone turned. He had already found the store room. Of course he had.

"Wet wall," he said.

Bessa said, "It doesn't leak."

"Wet."

"It's brick."

"Wet brick."

"That is what brick does in rain."

Davin looked at Teren.

"No."

Teren rubbed his face.

"Another room?"

Bessa pointed toward the side corridor.

"Office."

"Mine," said a voice from somewhere.

Bessa shouted back, "Not tomorrow." A man shouted, "Bessa!"

"Your desk can survive company."

"My papers cannot."

Davin said, "Box doesn't care about papers."

"Thank you," Teren said. "Useful."

I moved farther into the hall. The leak was not one leak. That became obvious quickly. Three buckets stood near the audience benches, but those drips were small and regular. The stage problem came from somewhere farther upslope. Water had traveled along something before appearing near the rear. I looked at the ceiling. Heavy rafters. Plaster between them in some sections. Exposed boards in others.

A dark line ran along one timber and disappeared behind the stage wall. Interesting. No. Not interesting. Work. I looked at the stage. The left entrance was unusable because the canvas and bucket occupied the path. The right entrance was dry. There was also a side door from the hall itself near the front benches. Audience entrance. Or actor entrance if necessary. Probably. I went closer. The gray-haired man climbed down from the stage.

"You with them?"

"Apparently."

He followed my eyes upward.

"Leak's not there."

"I didn't say it was."

"You're looking there."

"I was looking at the dark line."

"Old."

"Oh."

"Three years."

I looked again. He was right. The dark stain continued past the current wet area and had dust over part of it. Old. I had already been wrong. Good start.

"Current water comes from the west valley," he said. "Flashing lifted."

I looked at the roof from inside as if that would help. It did not.

"Can you fix it?"

"Yes."

"When?"

"When rain stops asking stupid questions."

Fair. He walked away. I liked him. Teren was now arguing about cancellation.

"If the stage is wet tomorrow, we don't perform."

Bessa said, "If you cancel tomorrow, I still have forty-two people who paid."

"You refund them."

"With what?"

"Their money."

"I used deposits."

Teren stared at her.

"For?"

"Hall."

"You own the hall."

"I manage the hall."

"Who owns it?"

"Three brothers."

"Where are they?"

"One dead. One south. One useless."

Marek whispered, "I like her." I said, "You like everyone who owes someone money."

"Shared values."

Teren said, "If we cannot perform because your roof leaks, I am not eating the loss." Bessa folded her arms.

"If you perform, you get your agreed share."

"If we cannot?"

"We move it."

"Where?"

She pointed toward the side wall.

"Assembly room."

The man in the office shouted, "No." Bessa shouted, "Not yours either." Teren looked toward the side corridor.

"How big?"

"Sixty standing."

"No."

"Seventy."

"You just said sixty."

"People get smaller when disappointed."

Marek nodded.

"True."

Teren ignored him. Bessa continued. "Or market shed."

"In rain?"

"Roof doesn't leak."

"Walls?"

"Two."

Teren closed his eyes. I started laughing. He opened them.

"Gregory."

"Sorry."

"You aren't."

"No."

He pointed toward the stage.

"Go see whether you can get from right wing to the house door without crossing the wet boards."

That was work. I went. The stage steps were at the right. I climbed them. The boards were worn smooth near center. My crutch tips held, but I tested before committing weight. Right wing. Dry. Rear path behind curtain. Mostly dry until the canvas began. Blocked. I came back.

The house-side door was below stage level, so using it meant coming down the right steps, crossing behind the front bench, and entering through the audience. Possible. Awkward. I tried it. Teren watched from the floor.

"Again."

I did it again. Not rehearsal. Geometry. The second time I caught my crutch on the edge of the front bench.

"Move bench," Teren said.

Bessa said, "That costs seats."

"One seat."

"Two if people don't want a crutch in their teeth."

"Move two."

Bessa looked at the forty-two imaginary coins already in her head.

"Fine."

Two local workers shifted the bench. That was it. Teren walked away. No scene. No lines. No Again beyond whether my body fit through the path. Professional preparation apparently consisted partly of making sure I could physically reach the place where I was supposed to lie about being a sword. Serra came onto the stage in her wet traveling clothes.

"Princess?" I asked.

"Tomorrow."

"I know."

She looked at the canvas.

"Where?"

"Right side. Maybe house."

She nodded. No complaint. Marek climbed up.

"King?"

Teren shouted from across the hall, "Tomorrow." Marek shouted back, "I am establishing geography."

"You are standing in the wet."

Marek looked down. One boot was on the canvas. He moved.

"Established."

Nessa entered carrying the red dress. Still unfinished. Also now wet at the bottom. Her expression could have stripped paint.

"Who," she said, "put the dress near the door?"

Nobody answered. Pell came in behind her.

"You did."

Nessa turned.

"I put it inside the door."

"Yes."

"The rain came inside."

"Yes."

"That is the door's fault."

Pell thought.

"Yes."

She looked at him suspiciously, as if agreement were another form of attack. Rinna brought a towel. The dress disappeared into the dressing room. The roof stopped mattering to them immediately. I envied that. Food arrived in two pots. I did not know who arranged it. Bessa maybe. Teren maybe. Rinna maybe. A local boy carried bowls. People ate wherever they were.

I sat on the edge of the stage, on the dry side, with stew balanced between my knees. Marek sat beside me.

"Drell."

"No."

"You thought it too."

"I was thinking about stew."

"You looked suspiciously."

"At stew?"

"Yes."

"What does suspicious stew look like?"

"This."

He pointed at my bowl. It did contain something I could not identify. I ate it. Potato. Probably. Marek lowered his voice.

"You think he wants you?"

I stopped chewing.

"That sentence is terrible."

"You know what I mean."

"No."

"Teren said he wasn't taking anyone."

"I heard."

"Why would he say that?"

"I asked."

"And?"

"Teren became Teren."

Marek nodded solemnly.

"A serious condition."

I ate.

"Do you know Drell?"

"No."

"You recognized the name."

"I recognized Teren recognizing the name."

"That is not the same."

"I am an actor. I work with implication."

"Fuck you."

"Good stew."

He stood. That was apparently the whole conversation. Fine. Drell remained in the previous town. Rain remained here. The rain was more useful. By full dark, the roof men were still working. The rain had softened to a mist. One climbed down for tar, or pitch, or something black in a pot. I went outside to see. Not help. See. The gray-haired man caught me.

"You."

"Me."

"Hold."

He handed me a lantern. I held it. He climbed the ladder. That was my contribution to roofing. The lantern. He called down, "Higher." I raised it.

"Not you. Lantern."

I raised the lantern.

"Better."

Another man on the roof pulled up the black material. I could see the roof shape now. The west slope met a short raised section over the stage. Water collected where two pitches changed. The repair was at the junction. I thought I understood.

"Valley catches too much from the upper section?"

The gray-haired man looked down.

"No."

"Oh."

"Gutter behind parapet blocked. Water backed under lifted flashing."

"Oh."

"Valley is fine."

"Right."

I held the lantern. Excellent. He had known his building longer than I had known the town existed. I shut up. Ten minutes later he said, "Now the valley might be a problem if that patch doesn't take." I looked up.

"Why?"

"Because then we send more water there."

"That sounds bad."

"It is."

"Can it carry it?"

He shrugged.

"Tomorrow tells us."

Buildings were rude. Eventually someone took the lantern from me because my hand had started shaking from holding it high. Not badly. Just tired. I went inside. Teren had found lodging. Or Bessa had. Or both. We were sleeping above a bakery two streets over. The smell was apparently free. The beds were not. Teren paid something. I saw coins move. Marek saw them too.

"Does that come out of us?"

"Company."

"Good."

"You are company when someone else pays?"

"I contain multitudes."

Teren pointed at him.

"You contain a hangover. Carry that crate."

Marek carried the crate. The hall settled into evening work. No rehearsal. Nobody ran Sword. Nobody ran Shopkeeper. Orin stood with Iven near the stage for perhaps three minutes discussing where one scene would enter if the left wing remained closed. They pointed. Iven walked the route once. Done. Serra and Marek did the same for another entrance. Serra walked through the house. A local woman moved a bench. Done. The experienced actors did not seem disturbed by this. I was. Not terrified.

Just aware that tomorrow we might perform an entire show in a room where one quarter of the stage was currently under canvas and one entrance had become two missing seats. I found Teren near the front doors.

"What if it still leaks?"

"Then we decide tomorrow."

"What if we use the assembly room?"

"We probably don't."

"Market shed?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Sound."

"Oh."

"And rain."

"It has a roof."

"Two walls."

"Right."

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You came over here."

"I had a question."

"You had four."

"Fine."

He turned back to the papers in his hand. I said, "Drell." His eyes closed.

"That was one."

"I know."

"Now it is five."

"Why did he know the box?"

Teren opened his eyes.

"Old company property."

That was more answer than I expected.

"What is in it?"

"I don't know."

I stared. He looked back.

"You don't know?"

"No."

"You own it."

"I own several things I don't understand."

"Why haven't you opened it?"

"Davin told me not to."

That was somehow the strongest possible reason.

"Why?"

"Ask Davin."

"I have."

"What did he say?"

"Dry."

Teren nodded.

"There you are."

"That is not an answer."

"It is Davin."

I leaned against the wall.

"So Drell knew the old company?"

"Yes."

"How?"

"Gregory."

"Yes?"

"Rain."

I looked outside.

"What?"

"Think about the rain."

"That is not how thinking works."

"It can be."

He walked away. I had learned exactly enough to become worse. The box belonged to the old company. Drell knew it. Teren knew Drell. Teren did not know what was inside. Davin did, perhaps. Or maybe Davin only knew how it needed to be stored. None of that helped with tomorrow. I went to the bakery. The lodging stairs were narrow and smelled like flour. Our rooms were smaller than River House and warmer. I shared again with Pell. He arrived ten minutes after me carrying the red dress.

"Finished?"

He looked at me.

"Sorry."

He put it over the back of a chair. The hem was still pinned in two places.

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"You said that yesterday."

"Yes."

"And before that."

"Yes."

"Do you know what tomorrow means?"

"No."

Fair. He sat on his bed and removed his shoes. One sock was wet. He stared at it as if betrayed personally. Then he lay down without changing.

"You're sleeping in wet socks."

"No."

"You are currently doing it."

He sat up.

"Fuck."

He changed the sock. I took my money from my inner pocket. Still there. Most of it. I counted once. Then put it away. Downstairs, the bakery ovens were still going. Someone laughed in the street. A cart rolled past. Rain tapped the window. Not hard. Enough. I thought about Lyssa. Not because anything dramatic had happened. Because I could imagine telling her about the hall. Not Drell first. The hall.

She would listen to me explain the roof for perhaps thirty seconds before asking whether I had been hired as a roofer. I would say no. She would ask why I had been on a ladder. I had not been on the ladder. That was important. I had held a lantern. Completely different. I smiled. Pell was already asleep. Of course. I lay down. The rain continued. Sometime later, someone knocked hard on our door. Pell did not move. I sat up.

"What?"

The door opened. Rinna. She held a candle.

"Greg."

"Yes?"

"Come downstairs."

I looked at Pell.

"Why?"

"Not him."

"That did not answer me."

"Teren."

I got my crutches. Downstairs, Teren stood in the bakery kitchen with Bessa, Iven, and a man I had not seen before. The stranger was soaked. Not theatrically soaked. Actually soaked. Water ran from his coat onto the floor. He looked sick. Or exhausted. Maybe both. Teren looked at me.

"Gregory."

No. I knew that tone now. Not the words. The shape. Something had become my problem.

"What?"

Teren held out several folded pages.

"You're also the Advocate tomorrow."

I stared at the pages.

"How many lines?"

Iven looked away. That was bad.

"How many?"

Teren said, "Forty-three." I stared at him.

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Night?"

"Yes."

"The show?"

"Yes."

"Forty-three?"

"Approximately."

"What does approximately mean?"

"Some are short."

I looked at Iven. He was enjoying this. Not kindly. Not cruelly either. Professionally.

"Who is the Advocate?"

The soaked man raised one hand.

"I was."

I looked at him. He coughed. Not a small cough. A deep, ugly one that bent him. He put his hand against the table until it passed.

"Oh."

"Yes," Teren said.

The man said, "Sorry." I did not know why he was apologizing to me. Maybe because forty-three lines had just crossed the room. I took the pages.

"Have I seen this scene?"

"Parts," Teren said.

"That is not the same."

"No."

"When do we rehearse?"

Nobody answered. I looked around. Bessa looked amused. Rinna looked tired. Iven looked at the pages. Teren looked at me. I understood. Of course. We didn't. Maybe tomorrow somebody would show me where to stand. Maybe Iven would tell me which lines actually mattered. Maybe Teren would cut ten. Maybe the roof would collapse and save me. Probably not. The rain tapped the bakery windows. I looked down at the first page.

ADVOCATE.

A lot of words followed. I read the first line. Then the second. Then looked up.

"Do I get paid more?"

Teren smiled.

"No."

"Fuck you."

"Learn the first page."

He left. Iven followed. Rinna took the sick man's arm and helped him toward a chair. Bessa went back into the rain. The bakery kept baking. The roof kept leaking somewhere two streets away. Tomorrow there might be a show. Apparently I was the Advocate.
# CHAPTER 156

## THE ADVOCATE

Forty-three lines was not forty-three lines.

This was the first lie.

I discovered it before I got back upstairs.

Iven took the pages from me, spread them across the bakery table, and
crossed out six.

"What are you doing?"

"Helping."

"You removed them."

"Yes."

"Those are my lines."

"Not anymore."

He crossed out another.

I took the charcoal from him.

"Stop."

"The joke is bad."

"That is not the point."

"It is one point."

The sick man who had been the Advocate sat wrapped in a blanket near the
ovens. His name was Lorn. I had learned that because Rinna had asked
whether Lorn wanted broth and he had said no before coughing for long
enough to reconsider.

He leaned over the pages.

"Keep the magistrate."

I looked at him.

"Which magistrate?"

Iven pointed.

"That."

"Why?"

Lorn said, "To arrest the Chancellor."

They looked at each other.

I said, "Excellent."

Iven tapped the page.

"Forgery first. Treason later."

Lorn said, "No. Treason accusation first. Forgery proves it."

"You've been saying it backward."

"I've been saying it for six months."

"Backward for six months."

Lorn coughed.

Then raised one finger.

"Paid."

I liked him.

The Advocate, as far as I could tell, existed because everyone else in
the play had committed too many crimes to explain them efficiently.

He entered after the Princess accused the Chancellor of falsifying a
royal order. The Advocate represented someone called the Merchant
Council, which had apparently lost three wagons because of the false
order. He brought a copy of the order, identified a seal, accused the
Chancellor of forgery, then argued with the King about whether the crown
could prosecute its own officer.

Later he returned to establish that the Chancellor had also redirected
soldiers away from a bridge.

That allowed Orin, playing the magistrate, to enter and arrest him.

Except Orin said treason.

Except Iven said forgery.

Except the pages contained both.

I read them again.

The words moved.

Not magically.

Tiredly.

"Who is the Merchant Council?"

Iven said, "Doesn't matter."

Lorn said, "Matters to me."

"You are the Advocate."

"Was."

"Fine. Why do I care about them?"

"You don't."

"Then why am I advocating?"

"Money."

Iven nodded.

Finally, a character I understood.

Lorn pointed at a paragraph.

"This matters."

It was eleven lines.

"All of it?"

"No. Seal. Three wagons. Bridge."

"The bridge is later."

"Right."

He closed his eyes.

Iven said, "Go to bed."

Lorn said, "I'm helping."

"You're dying on the bread."

"I am not."

Rinna put a bowl of broth in front of him.

He looked at it.

Then at her.

"Traitor."

"Drink."

He drank.

Iven took the charcoal back from me.

"First entrance. You need the order. You need the seal. You need the
wagons. You need to make Marek refuse to act."

"Why?"

"So Serra can force him."

"Why?"

"Because that is the scene."

"Useful."

He crossed out two more lines.

"Stop doing that."

"You won't learn them."

"I might."

"No."

That irritated me enough to try.

I took the pages upstairs.

Pell was asleep.

The red dress watched me from the chair.

I sat on my bed and learned the first page.

Not all of it.

I learned the beginning.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

Good.

Again.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

Again.

Then the next line.

Then the next.

The Advocate had too many nouns.

Merchants.

Order.

Seal.

Wagons.

Chancellor.

Authority.

Bridge.

Council.

Crown.

I learned a sentence about the seal and forgot which wagons had been
seized.

Three.

Three wagons.

I remembered three because Lorn had said three.

Then I forgot whether they carried wool or grain.

The page said wool.

The next page said grain.

I stared.

Pell snored.

I went downstairs.

Lorn was asleep at the table.

Iven was gone.

Rinna was gone.

The bakery woman was shaping dough.

"Wool or grain?"

She looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I went back upstairs.

Page one said wool.

Page three said grain because they were different wagons.

Of course.

I hated the Advocate.

I learned until the words became shapes.

At some point I woke with my cheek on the second page.

Morning had happened.

Pell was gone.

The red dress was gone.

I sat up too fast.

My neck hurt.

My mouth was dry.

The pages had lines from my face pressed into them.

I checked the window.

Gray light.

No hard rain.

Good.

Then I remembered forty-three lines.

Bad.

Downstairs, the bakery was full of people who had apparently decided to
have a day without waiting for me.

Nessa stood near the door drinking tea.

Serra was eating bread.

Marek was arguing with Bessa about tickets.

Davin carried a coil of rope through the room.

Teren was not there.

Iven saw me.

"First line."

I stopped on the last stair.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

"Second."

"That was one sentence."

"Second line."

I knew it.

I absolutely knew it.

Nothing happened.

Iven waited.

Serra ate bread.

Marek continued arguing about whether ninety people could become
ninety-two.

I said, "The order was presented at the south gate by men acting under
the Chancellor's authority."

Iven shook his head.

"North gate."

"Fuck."

"Doesn't matter."

"Then why correct me?"

"Because you asked."

"I did not."

He handed me bread.

"Eat."

Lorn was not there.

"Where is he?"

"Bed."

"Here?"

"Bessa's sister."

"Who is Bessa's sister?"

Iven looked at me.

"Exactly."

He left.

I ate.

The hall roof had mostly held.

That was the morning report.

Mostly.

One bucket remained near the left rear stage, but the canvas was gone.
The boards underneath were damp rather than wet. The gray-haired roof
man stood onstage in muddy boots while Teren pressed a heel against the
floor.

"Dry by evening," the man said.

Teren looked at the bucket.

"Mostly."

"Bucket's for confidence."

"Whose?"

"Mine."

Teren accepted this.

The left entrance might reopen.

Might.

Nobody restored the moved bench.

Bessa had sold eleven more tickets.

Fifty-three.

Marek knew before I did.

"Money," he said.

"People," Bessa corrected.

"People with money."

"People with tickets."

"Which were money."

"Yesterday."

Marek looked at me.

"She is difficult."

Bessa said, "You are standing in my hall."

"Beautiful hall."

"You called it a bucket with walls."

"That was before sales."

I went to the stage.

The route through the house remained open.

Good.

I could enter either way depending on whether the boards dried.

Bad.

Two possible entrances meant I now had two possible places to forget I
was supposed to enter.

Serra came up behind me.

"Advocate."

"Yes."

"Show me the order."

"What?"

"Your prop."

I looked around.

"I don't have it."

"Then you cannot accuse anyone of forging it."

"Where is it?"

She pointed toward props.

I went.

There were three rolled papers on the table.

One had a red ribbon.

One had blue wax.

One was blank.

I chose blue wax.

Pell, from the floor behind the table, said, "No."

I looked down.

He was sewing a shoe.

"Which?"

"Red ribbon."

"Why?"

"Blue is marriage contract."

"Whose?"

"No idea."

I took red.

Serra was gone when I returned.

Of course.

I put the order in my belt.

Then remembered the Advocate probably did not carry it in his belt.

I found Iven.

"Where do I keep this?"

He looked at the paper.

"Hand."

"For the entire scene?"

"Yes."

"What do I do with my crutches?"

He stopped.

That was useful.

We went back to the stage.

The Advocate had been written for Lorn, who had two legs and apparently
fewer logistical objections.

I could not carry the order and use both crutches while entering.

Iven tried tucking the paper under my arm.

It fell.

He tried my coat.

Wrong costume.

He tried rolling it tighter.

Nessa shouted from across the hall, "No."

We stopped.

She came over, took the order, and shoved it inside the front of my
Advocate coat.

I was wearing only the shirt.

"There."

"It will wrinkle."

"It is forged."

"Fair."

She left.

Iven said, "First line."

I said it.

"Seal."

I said the seal line.

"Wagons."

"Three wagons of wool were seized at the north gate under the
Chancellor's authority."

"Good."

"That is not the actual line."

"Good."

I looked at him.

He pointed toward the stage.

"King refuses."

I said the next part.

Wrong.

I made the King agree.

Iven stopped me.

"No. He refuses."

"I know."

"You just made him prosecute."

"I said he should."

"You said he did."

"Difference."

"Yes."

I tried again.

This time I forgot the Merchant Council.

Iven let me.

We reached the bridge.

I accused the Chancellor of diverting soldiers to the bridge.

"From," Iven said.

"What?"

"From the bridge."

I looked at the page.

That was worse.

If I said it wrong in the show, the Chancellor would have protected the
bridge instead of exposing it.

"Fuck."

"Yes."

I circled FROM with charcoal.

Then I circled NORTH.

Then THREE.

Then SEAL.

My pages began to look diseased.

Teren passed.

"How is he?"

Iven said, "Bad."

Teren kept walking.

I said, "Thank you."

"You asked?"

"No."

"Then why are you upset?"

Marek found out I had forty-three lines.

He was delighted.

Not because he wanted me to succeed.

Because he had fewer.

"How many do you have?"

"Enough."

"How many?"

"No."

"Orin does that."

"Good man."

"Help me."

"I am helping."

"You are drinking tea."

"Morale."

He drank.

I said, "King refuses to prosecute Chancellor."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Chancellor is his cousin."

I looked at the page.

"No, he isn't."

Marek frowned.

"Brother?"

"No."

"Then why do I care?"

"You are the King."

"You think I read the whole play?"

I stared.

He laughed.

"Ask Serra."

Serra was unavailable because someone had finally put her in the red
dress.

I knew because she came through the dressing-room door wearing it while
Nessa walked behind her staring at the hem.

Nobody celebrated.

Nobody announced completion.

The dress simply existed on a person.

Pell knelt, adjusted one pin, stood, and said, "Done."

Nessa said, "No."

Pell closed his eyes.

Serra looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're staring."

"The dress."

She looked down.

"Oh."

Apparently she had suffered less from it than everyone else.

"Why does the King refuse to prosecute the Chancellor?"

"Because if he admits the order is false, he admits he lost control of
his own seal."

That made sense.

"Also the Chancellor is his cousin."

I turned slowly toward Marek.

He raised his tea.

"I knew."

Serra walked away.

The day continued without respecting my problem.

Tickets reached sixty-one.

The roof man removed the confidence bucket, then put it back when a
brief shower came through.

Bessa swore at the sky.

Davin moved the long box from the office to a dry rear corner after the
office man demanded his desk back.

Rinna bought lamp oil.

I knew because I saw her pay two copper and complain about the price.

A local baker sent over a tray of small rolls because we were sleeping
above his ovens and apparently actors made his daughter laugh the night
before in another town.

That explanation made no sense.

Nobody refused the rolls.

Marek ate three.

A woman who had bought tickets brought Bessa a basket of pears "for the
players."

That was the phrase.

For the players.

Bessa took two pears as management tax.

The rest reached backstage.

I put one in my bag for later.

Five copper per show was money.

Pears were also money, in the sense that I did not have to buy a pear.

This seemed obvious enough not to require philosophy.

By afternoon I knew perhaps twenty-five lines exactly.

That number was misleading.

I knew another ten if someone gave me the first word.

I knew five in the wrong order.

I knew one from a completely different scene.

The remaining lines hated me personally.

Iven crossed out four more.

"You cannot keep removing the role."

"We are shortening."

"Teren know?"

"No."

"Teren!"

From across the hall:

"What?"

"Iven is cutting the Advocate."

"Good."

Iven crossed out another.

"Traitor," I said.

Teren shouted, "Gregory."

"Yes?"

"Learn less."

I hated everyone.

The sick Advocate's forty-three lines became thirty-two.

Then thirty-one because Orin refused to wait through a legal argument he
called "three minutes of furniture."

"It establishes jurisdiction," I said.

Orin stared.

"You have been Advocate for twelve hours."

"Thirteen."

"Dangerous."

He crossed out the jurisdiction.

I put it back.

He crossed it out again.

I let it die.

At some point, Bessa asked Teren whether we could add seats.

He said no.

She added four.

Teren removed two.

They settled on two.

Sixty-eight tickets.

The rain stopped.

The roof man climbed up once more.

The confidence bucket remained empty.

At five, Teren gathered us on the stage.

Not for rehearsal.

"Left is open unless it rains."

That was the meeting.

Nessa asked, "If it rains?"

"House route."

Orin said, "Rear cross?"

"Open."

Davin said, "No scenery on west brace."

Teren nodded.

Bessa said, "Seventy-one."

Marek smiled.

Teren said, "Good."

Then everyone left.

I stood there.

"That's it?"

Teren looked back.

"What?"

"We don't run anything?"

"Do you want to?"

I looked at the pages.

No.

"Yes."

"No time."

"Why did you ask?"

He walked away.

Doors in ninety minutes.

I ate stew.

Not enough.

Then too much.

I changed.

The Advocate coat was dark brown, too broad through the shoulders, and
smelled faintly of Lorn.

Nessa pinned one side so it did not bunch under my arm.

"Order."

I showed her.

"Good."

"Do I look like an Advocate?"

"No."

"Useful."

"You look nineteen."

"I am nineteen."

"That is the problem."

She went away.

I looked in the mirror.

She was right.

The Advocate probably should have looked like a man entrusted by
merchants to accuse royal officers of treason.

I looked like someone entrusted with holding a lantern.

Fine.

I tried the first line again.

Perfect.

Second.

Perfect.

Third.

North gate.

Three wagons.

Seal.

King refuses.

Crown cannot prosecute itself without admitting seal compromised.

Serra forces question.

Chancellor denies.

Forgery.

Bridge.

FROM the bridge.

Orin enters.

Arrest.

I could hold the shape.

Maybe.

The actual words remained less cooperative.

Doors opened.

I heard the audience enter.

Not all at once.

Feet.

Voices.

Wet coats.

Benches scraping.

Bessa telling someone no, their ticket did not include the front because
there was no front ticket.

Marek appeared beside me in costume.

"Money."

"How many?"

"Seventy-six."

"You asked?"

"Obviously."

"Is that good?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"More than seventy-five."

He left.

Iven came past.

"Order."

I showed him.

"Bridge."

"From."

"Good."

"King."

"Refuses."

"Seal."

"Compromised."

"Wagons."

"Three."

"Wool."

"North."

He nodded.

That was the most useful thing anyone had done all day.

Then he said, "You enter second scene."

"I know."

"You said third earlier."

I went cold.

"No, I didn't."

"Yes."

"When?"

"Lunch."

"I was wrong at lunch."

"Yes."

"Second."

"Yes."

"Fuck."

He left.

I stood behind the right wing.

The left entrance was open.

Dry enough.

The confidence bucket had been removed.

The first scene began.

I knew this part.

Not my part.

Good.

Marek entered.

Audience laughed at something he did before his first line.

Serra entered in the red dress.

It moved correctly.

Somewhere backstage, Pell whispered, "Done."

Nessa said, "Quiet."

I smiled.

Then remembered I was Advocate.

Second scene.

I checked the order.

Red ribbon.

Good.

The first scene ended.

People moved.

A prop table shifted.

Someone nearly knocked over a lamp.

Davin caught it.

I waited.

My entrance came after Serra's accusation.

I knew that.

I absolutely knew that.

Onstage, Serra accused the Chancellor of using the King's seal to seize
merchant wagons.

That was my entrance.

I did not move.

I was listening to the line.

Not entering.

Iven shoved my shoulder.

"Go."

I went.

Late.

Not terribly late.

Late enough that Serra had to look toward the wing as if summoning me.

I crossed onto the stage.

The hall looked different with people in it.

Seventy-something faces.

Warm lamps.

Wet coats steaming.

A child near the front.

Bessa against the rear wall.

My crutch struck the board once.

Too loud.

Marek looked at me.

King.

Right.

I reached into my coat.

The order stuck.

For one horrible second I fought my own costume.

Then it came free.

Wrinkled.

Forged.

Fine.

I looked at Marek.

First line.

Gone.

Completely.

The first line I had said perhaps fifty times.

Nothing.

The audience waited.

Marek waited.

Serra did not look at me.

I had the shape.

Merchants.

Order.

Seal.

I held up the paper.

"Your Majesty, three wagons belonging to the merchants of the eastern
road were seized at the north gate under an order carrying your seal."

Not the line.

Everything necessary.

Marek leaned back.

"And you have come to complain about my handwriting?"

The audience laughed.

That was not his line either.

Fine.

I said, "I have come because your handwriting is apparently stealing
wool."

Better laugh.

Dangerous.

I wanted the laugh again.

No.

Seal.

I broke the wax.

I was not supposed to break the wax.

Too late.

I held it out.

"This seal is yours."

Marek looked at it.

"Was."

What?

Serra moved slightly.

I saw it.

Not rescue yet.

My next line accused the Chancellor.

I knew it.

I said it.

Correctly.

The Chancellor denied it.

Good.

Marek refused to act.

Good.

Serra stepped in.

Good.

We were in the scene.

Then I said the wagons carried grain.

I knew immediately.

Wool.

The Chancellor actor looked at me.

Tiny pause.

He said, "Yesterday they were wool."

Audience laughed.

I stared at him.

Yesterday?

He had given me something.

I said, "Yesterday they were in our possession."

More laughter.

Not enough.

Necessary information still wrong.

I added, "Today the wool is gone, which is the complaint."

There.

Wool restored.

The Chancellor shrugged.

"Then perhaps you should advocate for better locks."

The scene moved.

I could feel my pages inside my coat.

Useless.

I could not read them.

I could not stop.

Marek refused.

Serra forced.

Seal compromised.

The first part survived.

Then I reached the bridge.

This mattered.

Soldiers had been diverted FROM the bridge.

I opened my mouth.

"To the bridge."

Fuck.

Orin was waiting somewhere.

The Chancellor smiled.

"Indeed. To defend it."

No.

I had reversed the crime.

The audience had no idea.

Everyone onstage did.

Serra looked at me.

Not panic.

Waiting.

I said, "They were ordered to the bridge."

The Chancellor said, "You just said that."

"Yes."

I could hear Iven backstage swearing.

I continued.

"They were ordered to it from the south road, then ordered away before
they arrived."

Was that the plot?

No idea.

Could become the plot.

The Chancellor actor said, "By whom?"

I held up the broken seal.

"You."

Silence.

Then Serra said, "Which is why the bridge stood empty when the
magistrate arrived."

There.

She had put the destination back where it belonged.

Orin entered.

Late or on time.

I did not know anymore.

He looked at the Chancellor.

Then at me.

Then at the broken seal.

"That was evidence."

I said, "It remains evidence."

"It is in two pieces."

"More evidence."

The audience laughed.

Orin took it from me.

"Stop helping."

That laugh was bigger.

I wanted to answer.

I did not.

Good.

Orin arrested the Chancellor.

The scene survived.

Not the scene on the page.

A scene.

When I came offstage, Iven caught me by the coat.

"From."

"I know."

"You said to."

"I know."

"You said it twice."

"I know."

"Good."

Serra passed us.

She was already going toward another entrance.

Without stopping, she said, "You owe me a bridge."

Then she was gone.

I looked at Iven.

"Is that bad?"

"Yes."

"How bad?"

He listened to the stage.

"Later."

He shoved the next prop into my hand.

I looked down.

A sword.

Not me.

An actual sword.

"What is this?"

"King."

"Why do I have it?"

"Because Marek needs it in twenty seconds."

"Why am I giving it to him?"

"You aren't. Put it on the table."

"Which table?"

Iven was already gone.

There were three.

The show continued.

Apparently the Advocate was only one of my problems.
