# CHAPTER 157

## THE PLAYER

There were three tables.

One held cups.

One held a crown, two folded letters, a wooden bird, and something that
might have been a dead fish.

The third was empty.

I put the sword on the empty one.

Pell appeared from nowhere.

"No."

"Fuck."

"Other."

"Which other?"

He pointed at the table with the fish.

"Why?"

"King."

"The King keeps his sword with a dead fish?"

"Not dead."

The fish moved.

I stared.

It was carved wood attached to a spring.

"Why does it move?"

Pell took the sword from me.

"Later."

"There is a later?"

He put it beside the crown.

"Hopefully."

Then he ran.

I had been offstage perhaps thirty seconds.

My Advocate coat was still pinned wrong under one arm. The broken order
was in Orin's possession. I had no idea where my pages were. Somewhere
onstage the Chancellor was being arrested for a crime I had nearly
transformed into public service.

Marek needed the sword.

I listened.

Wrong scene.

Not yet.

Good.

I leaned against the wall.

Iven came back.

"Why are you standing?"

"I am resting."

"Shopkeeper."

"When?"

He looked toward the stage.

"Two."

"Two what?"

"Scenes."

"That is not time."

"It is theatre."

He handed me a cloth cap.

I stared at it.

"Shopkeeper doesn't wear this."

"Tonight he does."

"Why?"

"Your Advocate hair."

I touched my hair.

It was hair.

Apparently it had become legally distinct.

I put on the cap.

Iven took it off.

"Wrong way."

"It's a cap."

"Yes."

He turned it and put it back.

I hated theatre.

The sword disappeared from the table.

Marek had apparently collected it without me noticing.

Good.

I started removing the Advocate coat.

Nessa caught the sleeve before I pulled.

"Pins."

"What?"

She reached inside and removed two pins.

"Do you want blood?"

"Not particularly."

"Then stop undressing like an animal."

She took the coat.

I stood in my shirt while she passed it to Pell.

"Shopkeeper coat."

Pell looked around.

Nessa said, "Pell."

"I know."

He did not know.

Neither did I.

The Shopkeeper coat was hanging behind the curtain because somebody had
moved the costume rail away from the leaking window. I found it after
Pell found something else.

He held up a gray coat.

"That is Marek."

"No."

"It was yesterday."

"Today it's Orin."

"Why?"

"Rain."

I stared at him.

He stared back.

Neither of us knew how rain had changed ownership of the gray coat.

Nessa shouted, "Shopkeeper!"

I found mine.

By the time I had it on, the audience was laughing.

I stopped.

Listened.

Still one scene before me.

Fine.

My body had begun doing something unpleasant where every sound from the
stage felt like a missed cue.

A door shut.

Was that mine?

No.

Audience laugh.

Mine?

No.

Serra spoke.

Definitely not mine.

I breathed.

I had done Shopkeeper four times.

This should have been easier than Advocate.

That thought was obviously a mistake.

Iven appeared in debtor clothes.

No coat again.

"The coat is gone."

"I see that."

"Good. Then I don't have to explain whose problem it became."

Fuck him.

We waited.

The hall was quieter than the eastern-town night crowd. Not silent. More
attentive. They laughed, but they did not shout over the play. Wet
weather had apparently produced people willing to sit indoors and watch
carefully.

I preferred the drunk ones.

They were less likely to notice legal errors.

Iven looked toward the wing.

"Go."

"Not yet."

"Correct."

"Why did you say go?"

"Testing."

"Fuck you."

He smiled.

Then our cue came.

We went.

Shopkeeper began well.

Not brilliantly.

Well.

Iven entered complaining about debt.

I asked how much he had.

He said less than yesterday.

I almost said, "Under whose authority?"

The words reached my teeth.

I stopped them.

The pause was too long.

Iven looked at me.

The audience looked at me.

I said, "That is an impressive way to answer without using a number."

A few laughs.

Not many.

Move.

Iven offered half.

I said, "Half is what people offer when they have all."

That was written.

I think.

He said he had expenses.

I asked whether I was one.

He said, "Increasingly."

Better.

Then I used the word jurisdiction.

I do not know why.

"Your poverty is outside my jurisdiction."

Silence.

Iven blinked.

I heard someone backstage choke.

I said, "Pay me."

That worked.

Not huge.

Enough.

Iven leaned closer.

"What is jurisdiction?"

"Expensive."

That worked better.

Fine.

Apparently the Shopkeeper had attended law school between towns.

The scene moved.

No uncle.

No aunt.

No coat.

No constable error.

Different room.

Different people.

At the end Iven tried to leave.

I said, "Where are you going?"

"To find a cheaper creditor."

"Bring him here."

"Why?"

"I have jurisdiction."

The audience laughed.

I hated myself.

Iven did too.

I could tell because he was trying not to smile.

Backstage he said, "Never again."

"Agreed."

"Jurisdiction?"

"I have been poisoned."

"By advocacy."

"Apparently."

He handed me water.

I drank.

The next scene was already moving.

Marek came offstage without the sword.

"Where is it?"

"What?"

"Sword."

"Gregory."

"No. Actual sword."

"Oh."

He looked back toward the stage.

"On throne?"

There was no throne in this hall.

There was a chair.

I looked.

The sword was not there.

Pell ran past.

"Sword?"

"Which?"

"Actual."

"Prop."

"Yes."

"Table."

"Which?"

He kept running.

I found the table.

No sword.

The wooden fish jumped.

I nearly hit it.

"Stop that."

The fish did not.

Iven appeared.

"Sword."

"I know."

"Where?"

"I don't know."

"Good."

"How is that good?"

"Now two of us know."

Serra came offstage in the red dress.

"What are you doing?"

"Looking for a sword."

She pointed.

It was under Marek's chair.

Of course.

"Why?"

Marek, from onstage, shifted his foot.

He had kicked it.

I retrieved it.

Serra took it from me.

"You need to be Sword."

"I know."

"You are holding Sword."

"That is different."

She shoved the prop into Iven's hands.

"King."

Then to me:

"Wall."

I went to the wall.

My Sword position had changed because the left entrance was open again
but the bench was still moved. The mounting board stood farther right
than in the eastern hall. My crutches went behind the flat. My body went
where it fit.

Someone strapped the decorative belt across me.

Not tightly enough.

I said, "Again."

The local worker tightened it.

"Good."

The scene before Sword ended.

I heard applause.

Then movement.

Serra entered.

Red dress.

Different room.

Different Princess.

Not because she had decided to become a new person, I thought. Because
the dress changed how she moved.

Or maybe I was making that up because I was tired.

She took me from the wall.

The belt caught.

For half a second, Sword refused to be stolen.

Serra pulled harder.

I came free.

Audience laughed.

She looked at me.

"Stubborn."

I said, "Evidence."

Wrong role.

A laugh anyway.

Serra's eyes changed.

Barely.

I knew.

I had brought Advocate onto Sword.

I corrected.

"I mean legendary."

Nothing.

Worse.

I should have left evidence.

Too late.

Serra said, "You are badly mounted."

"I was resisting theft."

"Poorly."

"I am a sword."

"That is your defense?"

"No. Apparently I need an advocate."

The audience laughed.

Fuck.

I had done it again.

Serra let the laugh pass.

Then:

"I have one. He's terrible."

Bigger.

I laughed.

Actually laughed.

Wrong.

She waited.

I stopped.

We continued.

Marek entered with the actual prop sword.

For one horrifying instant there were two swords in the scene, one of
them me and one of them sharp-looking wood.

He was not supposed to have it.

I knew because Serra looked at it.

Marek looked at it.

Then he looked at me.

"I found another."

Serra said, "Keep that one."

Marek looked at me again.

"Why?"

"This one talks."

Marek considered the prop.

He raised it to his ear.

The audience laughed.

He said, "This one has better manners."

I said, "That one has no jurisdiction."

Serra closed her eyes.

Iven made a noise backstage.

I had promised never again approximately six minutes earlier.

Marek said, "Neither do you."

Correct.

The scene continued.

The extra sword should have ruined something.

Instead Marek carried it until a servant character entered, then handed
it over without explanation.

The servant accepted it.

Gone.

Problem removed.

Later Serra gave me a line I knew.

I answered with the next line instead.

She looked at me.

I knew immediately.

I had skipped the setup.

The line I had said required her to have threatened the King.

She had not.

Audience silence.

Serra said, "I haven't threatened him yet."

Laugh.

I said, "I know you."

Bigger.

Then she threatened him.

We continued.

Backstage, she unstrapped me.

"You owe me two things."

"Bridge and threat."

"Good."

"Do I get credit for remembering?"

"No."

She left.

The rain started again during Orin's next scene.

I knew because everyone backstage looked upward at once.

Not audience.

Company.

A few drops hit the confidence bucket behind the left curtain.

Ping.

Pause.

Ping.

The roof man, who had stayed for the show, stood from his place near the
rear wall.

He watched the ceiling.

Ping.

Nothing.

Nothing.

Ping.

He sat back down.

Confidence restored.

The audience did not care.

One child turned around to look.

Bessa turned the child back by pointing at Orin.

Orin was in the middle of accusing somebody of poisoning somebody else.

He forgot the poison.

Not the accusation.

The object.

He reached toward the prop table.

No cup.

No jar.

Nothing.

I could see his hand from the wing.

He could see the empty space.

Pell whispered, "Blue."

I whispered, "Where?"

"Blue."

That was not location.

Iven looked under the table.

Nessa looked behind a trunk.

Orin continued speaking with his empty hand.

The other actor said, "You have no proof."

Orin looked at his hand.

Then at him.

"I had proof."

Audience laughed.

"Where is it?"

Orin looked toward the wing.

We all froze.

He said, "Stolen."

The other actor said, "Convenient."

"Crime often is."

They continued.

The blue poison jar was found thirty seconds later inside a boot.

Nobody knew why.

Pell blamed Marek.

Marek was onstage and therefore unavailable to defend himself.

Reasonable.

My second Advocate entrance came too soon.

Everything came too soon.

I had changed out of Sword but still had the Sword shirt under the
Advocate coat.

Nessa looked at it.

"No time."

"Good."

"No, bad. Go."

I had the pages this time.

I could not take them onstage.

I looked once.

Bridge.

From.

Seal.

Magistrate already knew.

This second entrance was shorter after the cuts. I returned to challenge
the King's attempt to dismiss the case after the Chancellor's arrest.
The Advocate had to establish that the forged order had caused actual
loss and that arresting one man did not restore the wagons or the
undefended bridge.

I knew the facts.

I knew them so hard I forgot the character.

I entered on time.

Excellent.

"Your Majesty, the soldiers were diverted FROM the bridge."

Too loud.

Too early.

That was not my first line.

Marek stared.

Audience stared.

I had walked onstage and announced a preposition.

Somewhere backstage Iven died.

Marek said, "I had gathered that."

I watched the knot.

Did not touch it.

Davin noticed me not touching it.

"Good."

That was all.

Orin was ready before Marek.

This disturbed everyone.

He had a coat today.

Both shoes matched.

The bruise on his jaw had darkened.

Marek stared.

"What happened to you?"

"No."

"You can't answer that with no."

"No."

"Was it furniture?"

"No."

"Was it attractive furniture?"

Orin climbed into the wagon.

"No."

Serra came from somewhere down the street carrying a small wrapped
parcel and the remains of the white flowers. Two blossoms had survived.
One was tucked through a buttonhole in her coat.

She said goodbye to nobody I knew.

A woman across the street raised two fingers.

Serra raised two back.

Then she climbed aboard.

Iven was annoyingly ready.

Pell was not.

Pell was missing.

We discovered this when Teren counted people.

Not loudly.

He looked at the wagons.

"Where is Pell?"

Nessa said, "Bakery."

We checked the bakery.

No Pell.

Rinna said, "Hall."

Marek volunteered to retrieve him.

Teren said, "No."

"Why?"

"You'll disappear too."

"Unfair."

"Accurate."

I went because I could not carry anything useful and therefore
apparently had time.

Pell was at the hall.

He was under the stage.

Of course.

"Why?"

"Fish."

I closed my eyes.

"The wooden fish."

"Yes."

"Why is it under the stage?"

"Don't know."

"Why do we need it?"

"Don't know."

"Then leave it."

He looked offended.

"It's ours."

That was apparently enough.

We found the fish wedged behind a support where someone had pushed it
with a boot.

Its spring still worked.

Pell carried it back like rescued livestock.

Bessa saw us crossing the square.

"One hundred!"

"No," I said.

"I wasn't asking you."

"Good."

We left at nine.

Approximately.

Nine according to Teren.

Marek said it was still morning and therefore exact time was oppressive.

The road east was better than the ridge road for the first hour, then
became worse in a more expensive way.

Stone paving appeared in stretches, cracked where wagon wheels had
broken the edges. Drainage ditches had been dug properly and then
neglected. Large houses appeared farther apart from one another behind
walls, hedges, or fields.

The rain held off.

That helped.

Marek slept.

That also helped.

I sat near the rear of the second wagon with Serra, Pell, and a costume
trunk that smelled faintly of damp wool.

The brass clasp remained in my inner pocket.

I checked once after a hard rut.

Still there.

My money was divided now. Most in the inner pocket. A few copper
somewhere easier to reach. The five from last night had joined the rest.

Serra noticed me checking.

"Rich?"

"No."

"Then stop touching it."

"I wasn't touching money."

She looked at me.

I stopped touching the clasp too.

Pell slept with his head against the costume trunk.

The wooden fish was on his lap.

Every large bump made it twitch.

After the fourth time I covered it with a cloth.

Serra said, "Coward."

"It watches."

"It doesn't have eyes."

I uncovered it.

It had painted eyes.

Serra looked.

"Fair."

We stopped once for water.

Teren spoke with Davin and Rinna away from the wagons. I could not hear.

Orin ate one of the stale rolls.

Marek woke long enough to ask whether we had arrived.

"No," six people said.

He went back to sleep.

By early afternoon the road narrowed between two stone walls.

The house appeared gradually.

First the gate.

Then trees.

Then a long pale roof beyond them.

Not a palace.

Too practical.

The main building had been expanded at least twice. The central portion
was older stone with tall windows and a steep roof. A newer brick wing
extended east. Another lower range connected to stables and service
yards.

I looked at the join between the stone and brick.

Teren, riding ahead, turned in his seat.

"We're not stopping for the wall."

"I was looking."

"Look fast."

The gatekeeper knew we were coming.

That was new.

At public halls we usually arrived and began proving we belonged there.

Here a man in a dark coat checked a written list.

"The players?"

Teren said, "Yes."

The man counted wagons.

Then people.

His eyes stopped on me for a fraction longer than anyone else.

Not rude.

Recognition.

"Good."

I did not like that word.

He waved us through.

The service yard behind the house was busier than the front had
suggested.

Cooks, stable workers, servants carrying linen, a boy rolling a barrel,
two women stripping leaves from herbs at an outdoor table, three dogs
who believed the wagons were personally offensive.

Nobody stopped working because actors arrived.

A woman in a dark green dress came down the service steps.

Not a servant, I thought.

Then she took a crate from the boy because he nearly dropped it.

Maybe.

She handed it to another worker.

"Teren?"

He climbed down.

"Lady Merra."

There.

Not servant.

Probably.

She was perhaps forty, with gray beginning at her temples and sleeves
plain enough to work in. She looked at the wagons before she looked at
us.

"You're late."

"Road."

"It's dry."

"Now."

She considered that.

"Fair."

Teren said, "Balance first."

She smiled.

"No."

"Then we're early."

"You're already in my yard."

"Still portable."

Marek woke.

He whispered, "Money."

Iven put a hand over his mouth.

Lady Merra heard anyway.

"Your king?"

Teren said, "Unfortunately."

She looked at Marek.

Marek removed Iven's hand.

"Majesty, privately."

"Not yet."

She looked back at Teren.

"Half after setup. Half after performance."

"You paid half already."

"Of the original."

"Which bought travel."

"Which bought arrival."

"Arrival happened."

"Setup hasn't."

Teren's expression changed slightly.

Not angry.

Working.

"What changed?"

"Guest count."

"How much?"

"Thirty-two."

"You said twenty."

"People marry."

Nobody reacted.

I looked at Serra.

She looked at me.

Lady Merra continued.

"My sister's daughter announced her engagement three days ago. The
dinner grew."

There.

Celebration.

Human-sized.

Teren said, "Thirty-two isn't a problem."

"The room is."

"Show me."

She did.

We entered through the service side, not the front.

The house was warm enough that my damp shirt became immediately
uncomfortable.

The performance room had probably never been intended for performance.

Long salon.

Polished floor.

Tall windows.

Fireplace at one end.

A small raised platform at the other, perhaps meant for musicians or
speeches.

Chairs were arranged in two shallow rows with tables behind them.

Too close.

Everything was too close.

I could have reached the front row with a crutch.

Marek whispered, "Excellent."

Serra said, "No."

The ceiling was high.

That was the only generous thing about it.

Teren walked the room once.

"Full play won't fit."

Lady Merra said, "I don't want the full play."

Of course.

"What do you want?"

"The King."

Marek straightened.

"The Princess."

Serra did not.

"The talking sword."

There.

Everyone looked at me.

I looked at the floor.

Lady Merra said, "And the creditor."

"Shopkeeper," I said.

"That."

Teren asked, "Who told you?"

"My nephew saw you in Carrow."

Which nephew?

Not important.

"He said the sword was a man with one leg."

There it was.

Not cruel.

Not even inaccurate enough to argue with.

Still.

Lady Merra looked directly at me now.

"You're Gregory?"

"Greg."

"Can you do both?"

I said, "Apparently."

Marek laughed.

Teren did not.

Lady Merra said, "Good. My father will like you."

That was worse somehow.

"Why?"

"He likes unusual things."

I looked at Teren.

Teren said, "No."

Lady Merra looked at him.

"No what?"

"No handling."

"I wasn't going to handle him."

"Good."

I looked at Teren again.

"Handling?"

"Later."

Lady Merra folded her arms.

"My father is seventy-one, half deaf, rude, and paying for the
engagement dinner. He likes performers who answer him."

"Answering is fine," Teren said.

"If he asks for another scene?"

"Depends."

"If he asks the sword to insult him?"

Marek said, "I can do that."

"No," Teren said.

Marek looked wounded.

Lady Merra smiled.

"What exactly did I buy?"

Teren began counting on his fingers.

"Forty minutes. Selected scenes. Six players. Music between if needed.
One additional piece if requested before we finish."

"An hour."

"Forty-five."

"Fifty."

"Food."

"Already included."

"For everyone."

She looked toward the yard.

"Actors and crew."

"Everyone."

"Fine."

"Wine?"

"For dinner guests."

"Beer?"

"For workers."

Marek whispered, "Workers."

Iven stepped on his foot.

Lady Merra said, "Fifty minutes."

"Forty-five plus one requested piece."

"Done."

"Balance before the requested piece."

She laughed.

"You are tiresome."

"Paid."

"Not yet."

They shook hands.

I had just watched Teren sell us without selling all of us.

That was interesting.

I did not say it.

The house steward appeared.

This man was definitely a steward because he looked offended by the
existence of unlisted objects.

His name was Harl.

He wanted the wagons moved.

Davin wanted the long box kept under cover.

Harl wanted nothing blocking the service arch.

They solved this without me.

The box went into a dry carriage bay, upright.

Nobody recognized it.

Nobody opened it.

Good.

"The actors can eat in the side room," Harl said.

I went with the actors.

Nobody corrected me.

The side room had a long table, bread, cold sliced meat, cheese, apples,
pickled onions, and a pot of something thick with barley.

Marek stopped in the doorway.

"Oh."

Rinna said, "Behave."

"I am."

"You haven't started yet."

The food was better than our last three meals.

Not impossibly better.

Just enough butter to reveal money.

The bread was fresh.

There was meat nobody had brought as a gift after a show.

There was more cheese than twelve people needed.

A servant set down another plate.

Rinna looked at it.

Then at the first plate.

Then at the servant.

"Does that stay?"

"Until dinner."

"And after?"

The servant shrugged.

"Kitchen decides."

Rinna nodded.

She had learned something.

Nessa touched the tablecloth.

Not dramatically.

Two fingers.

Then she looked at the curtains.

Pell followed her eyes.

"No."

"I didn't."

"You did."

"Fabric."

"Not ours."

"Obviously."

Marek had already found the beer.

Teren took it from him.

"After."

"I am a worker."

"Debatable."

Lady Merra entered before we finished eating.

"Change."

Teren looked up.

"What?"

"My father wants the sword at dinner."

"You bought after dinner."

"He wants it during."

"No."

She looked surprised.

Not offended.

Just unused to no arriving so quickly.

"It would amuse him."

"It would put Gregory between tables with people eating."

She looked at me.

I had not considered that.

Crutches, chairs, wine, servants, plates.

Bad.

"He can sit."

Teren looked at the salon again through the open door.

"At the end of the room."

"Near my father."

"End."

"Near."

"Then move your father."

She laughed.

Actually laughed.

"Nobody moves my father."

Teren said, "Then your father waits."

That could have gone badly.

Instead Lady Merra looked delighted.

"I see why my nephew liked you."

"He didn't see me."

"He complained about you."

"Better."

She left.

Marek said, "I want private money forever."

Teren gave him back his bread, not his beer.

Setup took less equipment and more thought.

No scenery.

Nothing tall.

No rear entrance.

The salon had two doors, but one led directly into a corridor guests
would use. The other led toward the side room.

Serra and Marek could use both.

I could not cross behind anything because there was nothing to cross
behind.

For Sword, they put my mounting board beside the fireplace.

I stared.

"Hot."

Davin moved it three feet.

"Better."

For Shopkeeper, a table and chair.

Lady Merra's steward wanted one of the house tables.

Teren said no.

Harl said ours looked poor.

Teren said, "Shopkeeper."

Harl looked at the battered table.

"Fair."

The guests began arriving before we were ready.

That was also different.

Public audiences waited outside.

Private audiences belonged to the building.

They wandered through.

A man with silver at his collar stopped to watch Pell pin a sleeve.

Two girls stared openly at me.

One whispered something.

The other whispered back.

Then both ran away.

A servant carrying wine said, "Sword?"

I said, "Sometimes."

He nodded.

"Good."

Again.

I was beginning to dislike being good before doing anything.

An older man entered using two sticks and no patience.

Seventy-one, presumably.

Lady Merra's father.

He had white hair, a heavy waistcoat, and the expression of someone who
had spent decades discovering that people eventually moved if he
continued forward.

Everyone moved.

He stopped in front of me.

Not close enough to be rude.

Close enough to inspect.

"You're the sword."

"Sometimes."

"One leg."

"Consistently."

He barked a laugh.

Good.

Not mine.

His.

"How'd you lose it?"

There were thirty possible answers.

None belonged in the salon.

I said, "Badly."

He laughed again.

Lady Merra appeared behind him.

"Father."

"What?"

"Don't interrogate the actors."

He looked at her.

"I'm paying them."

Teren appeared from the side room.

"You're paying for a performance."

The old man looked at him.

"Difference?"

"Several silver."

Silence.

Then the old man laughed harder than before.

"Fine."

He pointed one stick at me.

"Insult me later."

Teren said, "If the scene earns it."

The old man looked delighted.

I was less certain.

He walked away.

I said quietly, "Several silver?"

Teren said, "Not yours."

"Still."

"Work."

Then he left.

Forty-five minutes.

Selected scenes.

No Advocate.

Thank every god.

Sword.

Shopkeeper.

Marek's King.

Serra's Princess.

Orin in two short pieces.

Iven in Shopkeeper and another scene.

Music between.

One requested piece after payment balance.

This was not the play.

It was pieces of the play arranged around people who had eaten too much.

Dinner ran late.

Of course.

We waited in the side room dressed and ready while servants carried
plates past us.

The smell became cruel.

Marek ate another apple.

Nessa took it from him after one bite because his costume had pale
cuffs.

He finished it by leaning forward while she held it.

Nobody found this strange.

The household staff moved faster as the guests moved slower.

I watched a young servant balance six plates along one arm.

That was more impressive than anything I had done as Advocate.

When the salon finally cleared enough for chairs to turn toward us, the
guests brought wine with them.

Thirty-two had become thirty-five.

Harl looked offended by arithmetic.

Lady Merra looked pleased.

Teren looked at the room.

Then at us.

"Short."

"How short?" Marek asked.

"Until they stop listening."

"That is not time."

Iven said, "Theatre."

I hated him.

We began with the King.

Not me.

Good.

The guests talked through the first minute.

Not all.

Enough.

Marek pushed louder.

Teren, from the side, shook his head once.

Marek stopped pushing.

Serra entered.

The room changed.

Not silent.

More directed.

She had the red dress.

Apparently rich people liked red too.

Then Sword.

I was mounted beside the fireplace.

Three feet away from an old man holding wine.

Lady Merra's father.

Of course.

Serra took me.

The old man said, "That's him."

Serra looked at him.

Then at me.

"Apparently."

The room laughed.

That was not written.

Fine.

I said, "I was hoping for a less observant audience."

The old man laughed first.

Others followed.

Serra carried me into the scene.

Different distance.

Different danger.

I could see every face.

One woman was still eating a pear.

A man near the window whispered to someone through my line.

A child sat on the floor because chairs were apparently optional when
wealthy.

Serra asked what sort of sword complained about being stolen.

I said, "An expensive one."

Lady Merra's father called, "How expensive?"

There.

Customer.

Audience.

Patron.

Old man.

I looked toward Teren.

He did nothing.

That meant answer.

"More than your daughter told you."

The room exploded.

Lady Merra covered her face.

Her father slapped one stick against the floor.

Teren looked at the ceiling.

I had insulted him.

Apparently the scene had earned it.

We continued.

Not cleanly.

The old man interrupted twice more.

Serra answered one.

Ignored one.

Marek entered and immediately began playing to him.

That worked until it didn't.

The rest of the room started disappearing.

Teren coughed once.

Marek heard.

He turned back into the scene.

Interesting.

Shopkeeper came later.

The table looked poor enough to satisfy Harl.

Iven entered.

Lady Merra's father recognized me without the sword.

"Creditor!"

I said, "Unfortunately."

He said, "Charge him double."

Iven looked at him.

"Why?"

"Because I can afford it."

I said, "Then you're next."

That got him.

The room laughed.

Iven said, "Take him first."

"Older debt."

The old man raised his wine.

Fine.

The scene moved.

Private audiences did not know when to stay out of it because staying
out had never been part of the agreement.

That was the difference.

Or one difference.

A woman asked Iven directly whether his character had a wife.

He answered, "Not anymore."

I had never heard that.

Neither had he, probably.

She asked why.

He pointed at me.

"Debt."

I said, "I don't take wives."

"Good policy."

"Expensive."

Jurisdiction was dead.

Expensive survived.

Fine.

We reached the end.

Applause came from thirty-five people and six servants standing in the
corridor.

The servants were louder.

Marek bowed toward them.

Correct.

Lady Merra approached Teren before anyone could request anything.

She handed him a small purse.

He weighed it.

Opened it.

Counted.

Not secretly.

Silver flashed.

More than one.

Less than a fortune.

Enough that I understood why we had left Bessa's ninety.

Teren closed the purse.

Lady Merra said, "One more."

"One."

"My father wants the sword."

"Of course."

"Five minutes."

"Seven."

She blinked.

"You negotiate upward?"

"He'll interrupt."

She laughed.

"Seven."

Teren looked at me.

"Sword."

I said, "Do I get more?"

Lady Merra looked interested.

Teren said, "Two extra copper."

I stared.

"For seven minutes?"

"For requested piece."

Marek said, "I can be Sword."

"No," three people said.

Lady Merra's father shouted from the salon:

"Bring me the expensive one!"

I held out my hand.

"Two copper."

Teren put two copper into it before the scene.

That was new.

I pocketed them.

"Now?"

"Now."

I went back to the fireplace.

Apparently private money was different.

# CHAPTER 160

## THE SWORD

The two copper were still in my pocket when Marek put a crown on his
head.

"Why are you here?"

"Structure."

"You weren't invited."

"I am the King."

"That has stopped explaining things."

Serra stepped between us and took hold of the mounting strap.

"Seven minutes."

"Apparently."

"What are we doing?"

Marek said, "I sell him."

"No."

"I present him."

"No."

"I discover him."

"You already did."

Marek considered.

"Again."

Serra looked at me.

I said, "He paid."

Lady Merra's father struck one walking stick against the floor from
across the room.

"Expensive!"

The guests laughed.

Teren stood beside the side-room door with his arms folded.

He made a small circle with one finger.

Go.

Apparently that was the plan.

Serra lifted the strap from its hook.

"My father," Marek announced, already walking into the room, "left me
three things."

I stared at him.

That was not a line from anything I knew.

Marek continued.

"A crown, a kingdom, and a sword of incomparable worth."

Lady Merra's father called, "Which did you lose first?"

Marek stopped.

The room laughed.

He pointed at the old man.

"This is why kings have guards."

"Your guards are drinking in my kitchen."

One of the servants in the corridor laughed much too loudly.

Marek looked toward the sound.

"Betrayal."

Serra carried me forward.

I understood the shape now.

Maybe.

King had a sword.

Old man wanted sword.

Sword did not want old man.

That could last seven minutes.

Probably.

Marek held out a hand toward me.

"This blade has served my family for generations."

I said, "Against my will."

Lady Merra's father laughed.

"How much?"

Marek said, "Not for sale."

I said, "Finally."

The old man leaned back.

"Everything is for sale."

That landed differently.

Not bad.

Closer.

He was looking at me, not the mounting board.

I said, "Then you should be worried."

He smiled.

"About what?"

"Your daughter has already sold your evening."

Lady Merra closed her eyes.

The room laughed.

Her father looked delighted.

"Again."

There it was.

He pointed his stick at me.

"Say that again."

I almost did.

It had worked.

He wanted it.

He was paying.

The room was waiting.

Serra shifted the strap in her hand.

Not much.

Enough.

I said, "No."

The old man blinked.

"No?"

"I'm expensive."

The servants laughed first.

Then the guests.

Marek stepped in.

"He charges by the insult."

"I've already paid."

"Her."

Marek pointed at Lady Merra.

Lady Merra said, "Do not involve me in this."

"Too late," her father said.

Serra said, "Perhaps we should establish what exactly you're buying."

That sounded like Serra and Princess at the same time.

Good.

The old man looked at her.

"The sword."

"No."

"His insults."

"No."

"What have I bought?"

Serra considered.

"Seven minutes of regret."

That got nearly everyone.

I laughed too.

Fuck.

Only once.

I stopped.

The old man pointed his stick at Serra now.

"I like her."

Marek said, "She's not for sale."

Serra looked at him.

Marek corrected.

"She is not mine to sell."

"Better."

That laugh was smaller.

Not for the line.

For the correction.

I could feel the piece changing under us.

The old man was not a scene partner in the way Iven was.

He did not care what information came next.

He cared about what amused him now.

If we answered everything, we would stand there answering forever.

Marek tried to move.

"So, as I was saying, this sword has served my family for generations."

"Poorly," I said.

"Quiet."

"See?"

The old man laughed.

Marek continued before he could interrupt.

"It cannot be bought."

Lady Merra's father said, "Ten silver."

The room made a sound.

Not because it was real.

Because silver was silver.

Marek looked at me.

I looked at Teren.

Teren's face did not move.

Lady Merra said, "Father."

"What?"

"You're not buying an actor."

"I said sword."

I said, "That's how it starts."

A few people laughed.

The old man didn't.

He looked at me for a second longer.

"Twenty."

Lady Merra said, "Stop."

There was no anger in it.

There was enough authority.

He waved one hand.

"Imaginary money."

"Use imaginary silver," she said.

"That's what I was doing."

Marek said, "Then I demand fifty."

The old man looked offended.

"For him?"

"Legendary."

"I've heard him."

I said, "So have I."

That restored him.

He laughed.

Good.

Serra turned toward Marek.

"Your Majesty, perhaps you should demonstrate the blade's value."

No.

Absolutely not.

Marek looked at me.

"Cut something."

The old man slapped the arm of his chair.

"Yes."

I said, "No."

"Can't?"

"Won't."

"Can't."

"Won't."

"Can't."

This was becoming five-year-olds.

I could feel it.

The room liked it.

That made it more dangerous, not less.

Marek reached toward a bowl on a nearby table.

Teren said, "No."

One word.

Marek stopped.

The old man looked at Teren.

"Why?"

"House property."

"It's my house."

Lady Merra said, "Mine."

The old man turned.

"What?"

"You gave it to me."

"When?"

"Eight years ago."

"Bad decision."

"Yes."

That got the room without us.

Good.

Teren pointed at the wooden fish.

I had not noticed Pell had brought it.

Of course he had.

It sat on the edge of our battered Shopkeeper table, painted eyes
watching.

Marek picked it up.

"Fish."

Pell, from the side room, said, "Careful."

Marek ignored him.

He held the wooden fish toward me.

"Cut this."

I stared at it.

The old man leaned forward.

"Yes."

I said, "It's already dead."

The fish twitched.

Spring.

Perfect timing.

Not mine.

The room erupted.

I stared at the fish.

Marek stared at the fish.

Pell made a strangled noise from the doorway.

Lady Merra's father hit the floor with both sticks.

"Again!"

"No," I said.

This time immediately.

Bigger laugh.

The fish had done more work than I had.

Marek set it down carefully.

"Legendary mercy."

"Professional caution."

The old man pointed at me.

"What are you when you're not a sword?"

There.

Closer again.

I knew what he meant.

Maybe.

The room changed only because I did.

Serra answered before I had to.

"Off duty."

The old man looked at her.

"I asked him."

Teren unfolded his arms.

Lady Merra said, "Father."

I could have let them end it.

Instead I said, "More expensive."

The old man laughed.

The room came back.

Fine.

He accepted the door I gave him instead of the one he had opened.

"Everything costs more here."

Lady Merra said, "You live here."

"Exactly."

Marek took the opportunity.

"And that is why the sword cannot be sold."

I said, "Because he couldn't afford me?"

"Because I cannot afford to replace you."

That was better.

I looked at him.

"Almost kind."

"Don't tell anyone."

Serra hung the strap back on the mounting hook.

That felt like an ending.

The old man said, "Wait."

Of course.

Teren looked toward Lady Merra.

Lady Merra looked at her father.

"One."

He thought.

Then pointed at Marek.

"Insult him."

Marek said, "No."

I said, "He dresses like a king."

Silence.

Then the old man laughed so hard he coughed.

Marek stared at me.

"That's not an insult."

Serra said, "It was."

The room broke again.

Teren stepped forward.

"Seven."

Done.

Lady Merra's father called, "Eight!"

Teren said, "Two more copper."

The old man laughed.

"No."

"Then seven."

That was the end.

Not because the old man stopped wanting more.

Because Teren ended it.

We bowed.

The servants in the corridor applauded.

One of the little girls had come back and was sitting on the floor
beside the door. She clapped the wooden fish against her palm until Pell
took it away from her.

"Careful."

"It bit me."

"It doesn't bite."

The fish twitched.

She dropped it.

Pell caught it against his chest.

"See?"

I came off the mounting board.

My shoulders had gone tight from sitting wrong.

Serra helped with the strap, then immediately left because Lady Merra
wanted her.

Marek followed the old man toward the drinks.

I sat for a moment.

Teren passed.

"Two copper."

"I know."

"You asked."

"I know."

"Good."

"Was that good?"

He kept walking.

"Paid."

I hated him.

Private performances did not end backstage because there was no
backstage.

They ended while the people who had watched you were still in the room.

A man in a dark blue coat came over while I was putting my crutches
under me.

"That fish."

"Not mine."

"Does it always do that?"

"I hope not."

He laughed.

"You're the Advocate too?"

Apparently someone had been talking.

"Sometimes."

"I saw something like that play in Carrow ten years ago."

"Not with me."

"I gathered."

He started telling me about it anyway.

Different King.

Different company, perhaps.

Or same name.

I did not know.

His wife came and rescued me by taking him away to say goodbye to Lady
Merra.

Then one of the girls asked if the sword slept.

"Constantly."

"Where?"

"Wall."

"Which wall?"

"Whichever pays."

She considered this.

"That's stupid."

"Yes."

She left satisfied.

I found the side room.

Rinna had already begun converting rich-house abundance into road food.

Not stealing.

I checked.

A kitchen woman was handing her wrapped parcels.

"These go bad tomorrow."

Rinna nodded.

"These?"

"Keep."

A loaf.

Half a cold roast.

Cheese ends.

Six apples.

Something wrapped in leaves.

Rinna opened it.

Cakes.

Marek appeared.

Rinna closed it.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"You arrived."

The kitchen woman laughed.

"Give him one."

Rinna looked betrayed.

Marek received a cake.

"Private money," he said through it.

"That's not money," I said.

He swallowed.

"Better."

The kitchen woman handed me one too.

I accepted.

Fine.

Maybe better.

Harl came through with a list.

"Nothing from the upper rooms."

Rinna said, "We weren't in the upper rooms."

"Nothing from the east gallery."

"We weren't there either."

"One silver spoon is missing."

Marek stopped chewing.

Every head turned toward him.

He looked offended.

"I don't steal spoons."

Orin, from the corner, said, "Professionally."

Marek pointed at him.

"Exactly."

Harl did not appreciate this.

Teren appeared.

"Search our things."

Harl looked surprised.

"So quickly?"

"Yes."

Marek said, "Wait."

Teren looked at him.

Marek reached into his costume coat.

Everyone became very still.

He pulled out an apple.

Then another pocket.

A folded handkerchief.

Another.

Two corks.

"Why?" I asked.

"No."

"That's Orin."

Marek checked his last pocket.

Empty.

"See?"

Harl looked unconvinced.

A servant came in holding the silver spoon.

"Found it."

"Where?"

"The garden."

Silence.

Harl closed his eyes.

"Why?"

The servant shrugged.

"Master Olan."

Lady Merra's father.

Of course.

Harl left without apologizing.

Marek said, "I demand compensation."

Teren gave him the apple from his own pocket.

Marek accepted.

The silver purse moved.

I saw it because Teren took it out while Rinna was tying the food
parcels.

He counted three silver into her hand.

Not all of it.

Three.

Rinna put two into one cloth packet and one into another.

"Wheel," she said.

Davin, passing the doorway, said, "Yes."

"Food."

"Yes."

"East toll?"

"Maybe."

Teren gave her several copper too.

She counted them.

Then he closed the purse and put it back inside his coat.

That was enough explanation.

The money had already started becoming road.

Teren called names.

Payment.

My name came after Pell.

"Gregory."

I went over.

He put six copper into my hand.

I counted.

"Six."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Private rate."

"I had three roles."

"Selected work."

"Six."

"Yes."

"And two extra."

"Already paid."

"Eight total."

"You're learning."

I looked at the coins.

Public show, five.

Private selected performance, six.

Requested extra, two.

Eight copper for the day.

No silver.

Still more than I had earned from one show before.

Marek leaned over my shoulder.

"Rich."

"Go away."

"What did you get?"

"Eight."

He frowned.

"I got six."

"You didn't do extra."

"I was in extra."

"You invited yourself."

"I provided structure."

Teren said, "You provided crown."

Marek looked at him.

"One copper."

"No."

"Half."

"No."

"Cake."

"You already had one."

"Then paid."

He walked away.

I put the six copper with the two.

Eight.

Then checked the clasp.

Still there.

Good.

Serra returned with Lady Merra.

Lady Merra had removed her formal outer layer and rolled her sleeves
again.

"Sleeping."

Teren looked at her.

"Here?"

"Stable loft and two service rooms. Unless you'd prefer the village
inn."

"Cost?"

"Included."

"Food morning?"

"Included."

Marek shouted from somewhere, "Excellent house!"

Lady Merra ignored him.

Teren said, "Done."

That easy.

No one had to spend today's pay on a bed.

That mattered more now that I had enough money to notice keeping it.

The stable loft was clean by stable standards.

Hay smell.

Wood.

Dust.

No horses directly below us, only tack and an empty stall.

The service rooms went to people with costume trunks and people who had
already claimed them by moving faster.

Pell and I got the loft.

Again.

He brought the fish.

"Why?"

"It's ours."

I accepted defeat.

Before sleep, though, there was beer.

Worker beer.

The household had a long table in the service yard under an awning.
Stable hands, kitchen workers, two servants, Davin, Rinna, Orin, Iven,
Marek, Serra, Pell, Nessa, me.

Teren came later.

Lady Merra did not.

Her father did.

Of course.

He appeared at the top of the service steps in a different waistcoat
with one stick instead of two.

Harl followed him looking exhausted.

"Beer," the old man said.

Harl said, "You have wine."

"Beer."

A stable hand gave him beer.

Class structure survived approximately three seconds.

He sat at the end of the table.

Not beside me.

Good.

He talked to Davin about wheels.

Davin answered more words than I had heard from him all week.

Not many.

Enough.

Apparently the old man knew something about axle wood.

Or pretended convincingly.

I could not tell.

I drank one beer.

Food came again because apparently this house did not understand
scarcity.

Cold meat.

Bread.

Onions.

The leaf-wrapped thing turned out to be soft cheese with herbs.

Rinna had already packed most of it for tomorrow and allowed us only
one.

Marek complained.

Rinna said, "Road."

He said, "Today."

"Road tomorrow."

He lost.

Serra sat across from a kitchen woman I had not met and spent ten
minutes talking about someone named Seli who had married badly and knew
it.

I did not know Seli.

Nobody explained.

Orin played dice with two stable hands.

His bruise was none of their concern.

Pell demonstrated the wooden fish to the little girl from the salon.

It bit her.

Apparently Pell had lied.

She screamed, then laughed.

He showed her how the spring worked.

I looked away before I learned too much.

Teren sat beside Rinna.

A man from the dinner came out to find him.

Not blue coat.

Another.

Broad, trimmed beard, good boots.

They talked standing.

I heard only pieces.

"East."

"Two days."

"Harvest fair."

"Hall?"

"Square."

"Weather."

"Covered market."

Teren asked something.

The man named a place I did not know.

Teren said, "When?"

"Six days."

Teren looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked toward Davin.

Davin was still talking axle wood with the old man.

She said, "Possible."

Not yes.

The bearded man gave Teren a card or folded paper.

Teren put it away.

Work traveling through dinner guests.

No announcement.

No destiny.

Maybe another job.

Marek noticed.

"Money?"

Teren said, "Sleep."

"Is sleep money?"

"No."

"Then wrong answer."

The old man laughed from the end of the table.

"Keep the king."

Teren said, "Please don't."

Later, when the yard had emptied somewhat, Lady Merra came out.

She thanked Teren.

Then Serra.

Then Marek.

Then me.

Not separately because I was special.

She was going down the table.

"Father enjoyed himself."

"I noticed."

"He'll tell everyone he bought the sword."

"He didn't."

"I know."

She looked toward the old man, who was now arguing with Harl about
whether he could sleep in the stable.

"He won't."

"Good."

She started to go.

I asked, "Your nephew?"

She turned.

"The one who saw us in Carrow."

"Jerin."

"Why did he remember me?"

She looked at me for a moment.

"Because you were funny."

That was almost disappointing.

"And?"

"And you had one leg."

There.

Simple.

"Right."

"He described Marek as the loud King."

From the table Marek said, "Accurate."

"He described Serra as the woman who made the King look stupid."

Serra raised her beer.

"Accurate."

Lady Merra said, "People remember what they can describe."

Then she left.

I sat with that for perhaps half a minute.

Marek leaned over.

"I can describe you."

"Don't."

"Expensive sword."

"That's two words."

"Efficient."

Serra said, "Loud King."

Marek looked hurt.

I finished my beer.

The brass clasp in my pocket pressed against my hip when I shifted.

Lyssa would have liked Lady Merra.

Maybe.

Or she would have liked watching Lady Merra tell her father no.

More likely.

I wanted to tell her about the silver spoon in the garden.

That was better than Drell.

Better than the box.

Better than most things.

I climbed to the loft.

Pell was already there.

The fish sat between our bedrolls.

"No."

"It can't sleep by the wall."

"It is wood."

"It's ours."

I moved it to his side.

He moved it back.

We compromised by putting it at his feet.

Outside, the estate settled.

Doors shut.

A horse stamped.

Someone laughed in the service yard.

The old man's voice carried once, then Harl's, then neither.

I counted today's eight copper in the dark by touch.

Not because I needed to.

Because I could.

Five had felt like proof that the show had happened.

Eight felt like something else.

Not wealth.

Work with different terms.

Tomorrow the bed cost nothing.

Breakfast cost nothing.

Rinna had food packed.

Three company silver had already become wheel, food, maybe toll.

Somewhere east there might be a harvest fair in six days.

I put the coins away.

The clasp stayed wrapped.

The letter kept going south without me.

Down below, someone closed the carriage bay.

The long box remained dry.

I slept.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
